There is no shortage of ways to redeem your points and miles for travel to Europe. With most flights being overnight, booking a lie-flat seat is an excellent way to ensure you arrive rested and refreshed on the continent.

Points and miles enthusiasts usually need to choose between paying high redemption rates or high surcharges. Programs like Delta SkyMiles charge just $5.60 in taxes and fees for business-class flights to Europe but expect up to 500,000 miles per person for flights as short as seven hours on peak dates.

Many European programs have much lower redemption rates, such as British Airways Club, which charges just 88,000 Avios for a one-way, off-peak flight to London from the Northeast. The trade-off is you will need to stump up almost $500 in taxes, fees and surcharges to BA.

The Scandinavian Airlines EuroBonus program charges just 60,000 EuroBonus points for a one-way, SAS-operated Business Bonus award between North America and Europe. The cherry on top? You'll need to pay just $5.60 in taxes and fees. Although this loyalty currency has traditionally been difficult to earn, thanks to the new Rove transfer option, you can fly to Europe for less than the price of a cup of coffee in taxes and fees by redeeming miles.

Related: Earning 28 miles per dollar: How a 2-night New York City hotel stay earned me enough miles to fly to Europe using Rove

Here's how to do it and what my experience was like.

SAS doesn't add carrier-imposed surcharges to awards on flights it operates, making SAS EuroBonus one of the best-value Rove transfer partners for business-class travel to Europe.

SAS flies nonstop to Copenhagen Airport (CPH) from the following U.S. gateways, although some routes are seasonal:

SAS also flies nonstop from Newark to Oslo Airport (OSL) and Stockholm Arlanda Airport (ARN).

Related: SAS has brought back European Business class on short-haul flights

Business Bonus seats at the fixed 60,000-point rate were strictly limited and were not available on every route or date I searched. When they were unavailable, SAS displayed regular fares that could be paid with points at a much higher rate, so flexible dates helped a lot.

Rove miles transfer to EuroBonus points at a 1:1 ratio, with a 2,000-mile minimum and transfers in increments of 100 miles. My transfer posted instantly, though Rove says transfers usually complete within one day.

Transfers can't be reversed, so the golden rule applies here: Find award space you're happy with before you move a single mile.

SAS award flights booked on the website must currently be reserved at least three days before departure. The SAS app allows closer-in bookings, but for reservations made within three days of departure, the EuroBonus member must be traveling.

Taxes and fees were higher on the way back. When I checked, a SAS business-class award from Copenhagen to the U.S. required about $95 one-way.

Related: A game of thrones: Flying business class on Scandinavian Airlines' A321LR from Copenhagen to Washington

EuroBonus isn't the only option to redeem your Rove miles to fly to Europe. Other transfer partners can be used, but the combination of redemption rates plus taxes, fees and surcharges is not as attractive as EuroBonus:

Related: How to avoid paying fuel surcharges when redeeming points and miles

My journey to Europe began by purchasing a tall latte from Starbucks at ATL for $6.16, including Georgia sales tax, more than the taxes and fees I paid for my business-class flight.

I then used the Sky Priority check-in for my flight to Copenhagen, which allowed me to check two bags, each up to 70 pounds.

SAS business-class tickets to Europe include access to Delta Sky Club lounges. SAS departs from Concourse F, one of the two international concourses at Atlanta Airport, so I headed to the Sky Club in this concourse.

Related: A posh Delta One lounge is coming to Atlanta

It featured an outdoor terrace, which was a great place for planespotting and soaking up the Georgia sunshine.

A kindly staff member who noticed my photo-taking gave me a tip that there was a newer and more luxurious Sky Club in Concourse D I could access on the same ticket. Since I still had several hours before my flight, I headed over there.

It was a big, bright room with floor-to-ceiling windows on both sides looking out over the airfield, and the green and teal decor was a nod to Atlanta's "City in a Forest" nickname.

Based on my visit, I would recommend heading to Concourse D if you have time; I preferred its newer, larger space.

Related: Inside Delta's brand-new Sky Club in Atlanta, its nicest one yet

There were plenty of hot and cold food options available, which is ideal for anyone heading to Europe and wanting to maximize their rest on their flight.

Despite being busy during the late afternoon and early evening, the bartenders happily served up sparkling wine, beers and soft drinks and well as whipping up cocktails and chatting to guests about their travel plans.

After taking advantage of priority boarding for business passengers, I boarded the SAS Airbus A350-900, which had 40 business-class seats in a 1-2-1 layout, so every passenger had direct aisle access.

The cabin had a calm, understated palette of charcoal gray seat shells with brushed silver trim and blue-flecked gray fabric, with a tan, leather-look panel lining each side console to warm it up.

The bedding was already at my seat when I boarded, wrapped in plastic. It came from Dux, the Swedish bedmaker that was SAS's official comfort partner at the time, and included a gray and white pinstriped duvet and two pillows.

The amenity kit was a limited-edition one for SAS’s 80th anniversary. It came in a navy zip pouch with the airline’s 80 logo on the front. Inside was a matching navy eye mask, earplugs and a dental kit, plus lip balm and hand cream from Swedish skincare brand Muro Scents.

A pair of SAS-branded over-ear headphones hung on a hook in the side console. There was a universal power outlet and a USB port right next to it, and the seat itself was controlled from a touchscreen panel, including lumbar support.

I was more interested in sleep than cinema on my flight to Denmark, but the 18.5-inch touchscreen had a solid selection of recent releases, including "The Devil Wears Prada 2."

The drinks list was where SAS leans hardest into its Scandinavian roots.

Alongside Charles Heidsieck Brut Reserve Champagne, there was a hazy IPA brewed by Danish brewery Mikkeller in collaboration with SAS; two SAS-exclusive spirits, Herno Old Tom Gin and High Coast whisky from Sweden; and a cocktail menu that included the SASmopolitan.

For my Atlanta departure, the menu had a definite Georgia flavor. The starter options were grilled peaches wrapped in prosciutto with mozzarella and balsamic pearls or seared ahi tuna. Main courses included smoked beef short rib with stone-ground grits from Georgia's Riverview Farms, a hot honey-glazed chicken thigh and goat cheese and apple ravioli.

I chose the ahi tuna, which was a light and fresh start to the meal, with a hearty slice of sourdough bread on the side.

For the main course, I went for the beef short rib, an indulgent and delicious option with super-tender beef and creamy grits.

With a fairly short flight time and a full stomach, I skipped dessert, reclined my seat fully flat and settled in for the night.

The crew set up a snack bar for business-class passengers who got hungry during the flight, but most focused on getting a good night's rest.

I slept right through breakfast (the crew had asked at dinner whether I wanted to be woken) and arrived refreshed and ready to explore the charming city of Copenhagen.

After years of having to choose between high redemption rates and high surcharges, booking through SAS EuroBonus could be the ultimate sweet spot to Europe.

I've flown plenty of business-class products across the Atlantic, and SAS offered a very respectable experience on the A350 with friendly staff, direct aisle access, comfortable bedding and some fun Scandic touches.

Joining Rove costs nothing, and you can earn 1,500 bonus miles when you sign up through TPG's link. As an added bonus, new users can earn an additional 5,000 miles after making their first hotel booking of $500 or more with code "BRIANKELLY500".

I'd much rather pay $5.60 for a lie-flat seat to Europe than a cup of coffee. How about you?

#6237. Avelo Brings First Commercial Flights to McKinney

Avelo operated its inaugural flight from McKinney National Airport in McKinney, Texas, on Wednesday.

Avelo Flight 1848, operated with a Boeing 737-800, was the first commercial airliner service from the airport to Fort Myers, Florida.

“We target the secondary airports of very large metropolitan areas where we can offer a different experience to the customers,” Avelo founder and CEO Andrew Levy said in an interview with AirlineGeeks.

McKinney is the third airport in the Dallas/Fort Worth Metroplex to offer commercial service, with Dallas Love Field and Dallas/Forth Worth International Airport being the other two.

“For a lot of folks we’re going to be closer and a more convenient drive. And hopefully they’ll take advantage of that,” said McKinney airport director Ken Carley.

Carley said the airline has been wanting to be in the market since 2018. McKinney is the first new airport in Texas in 20 years to be certified for commercial air service.

“We had to build all this infrastructure because it did not exist. There was nothing on this side of the airport. So it’s not just this building, it’s the ramp and the taxi lane and all of that stuff, the taxiway that connects to the runway system. So it was a building, all the infrastructure, and meeting all those requirements,” Carley said.

McKinney is about 30 miles northeast of Dallas in Collin County. Levy said the area is growing like crazy.

“What we’re going to offer people who live close to this airport is a very different experience than getting on the highways and driving all the way to DFW or going down to Love Field,” he said.

The Texas-based airline will serve 11 destinations from McKinney: Las Vegas, Tampa, Orlando, Fort Myers, Sarasota/Bradenton, Nashville, West Palm Beach, New Orleans, Denver, Atlanta, and Fort Lauderdale.

“I think it’s phenomenal that Avelo has announced additional routes before they’ve even started service. That’s a testament, I think, to what they’re seeing in the response they’re getting from for bookings. So they think it’s a strong market,” Carley said.

Levy said the approach was to offer a lot of selections and get a better sense of the market.

“All the markets we’re serving have massive proven demand from this area. And so of course, the trick for us is just to get people to know we’re here and then give us a try,” Levy said.

McKinney is a crew base for Avelo, its fifth, with pilots, flight attendants, airport operations personnel, and aircraft technicians, about 150 people behind the operation, Levy said.

“The demand will dictate how we grow, if we grow, and how fast we grow. This is going to be based on, do customers like the service? Does it resonate with them? Are we serving a need that exists every other place we’ve been? We don’t have any trouble filling up airplanes. I think this market is just going to do great, but time will tell, and the consumer will let us know,” Levy said.

“Our focus is on building a business that’s sustainable for the long term,” he added. “And that means everything we do has to work. It’s got to work well.”

Avelo currently offers service from DFW to New Haven, Connecticut. Levy said that service will continue but could move to McKinney at some point.

#6236. Why Russia Is Targeting European Freezers

Rearmament isn’t just for the battlefield — civil defense matters, too.

A woman walks past partially empty shelves at a SuperValu store in Blanchardstown, Dublin, Ireland, November 2, 2026.

Twice in the space of a few weeks, Russian hackers have managed to seize control of supermarket refrigeration systems in Europe. It began with hundreds of French stores in mid-October, after which, in early November, hackers struck outlets in Sweden, Belgium, Ireland, the Netherlands, and elsewhere. The hackers remotely forced freezers and chillers into prolonged defrost mode, driving temperatures to more than 120 degrees Fahrenheit and spoiling large quantities of food. These attacks have revealed an underrated aspect of rearmament that has so far been almost completely overlooked: civil defense.

Hackers behind most ransomware attacks demand payment. These hackers simply disrupted Europe’s food supply and left without a message. Only a few days after the most recent (as of this writing) attacks, in early November, did a Russian group finally claim responsibility. European policymakers who may have wished that some random teenagers were behind the attacks instead had their fears confirmed: This was a Russian attack against Europe’s food supply.

‘Tis the season … when frequent flyers scramble for eleventh-hour ways to qualify for airline elite status they haven’t quite reached yet.

If Southwest is your airline of choice, the end of 2026 is particularly important to hit status milestones, as Southwest’s Rapid Rewards program is about to change in major ways in early 2027.

With fewer international flight options and no premium cabins for upgrades, chasing Southwest status might not seem as necessary as it does with larger competitors like United Airlines or Delta Air Lines.

But if you fly Southwest a lot and are close to hitting a status goal, it’s wise to explore easy and inexpensive ways to get over that hump.

What you need to do to earn status depends on what part of Southwest’s program you are targeting. Southwest technically has two official status tiers in 2026. Plus, members who fly (or spend) the most can unlock its popular Companion Pass.

Coming next year: Commonly asked questions about Southwest's recent Rapid Rewards reboot and Companion Pass changes

You can check how close you are to status by logging into your Rapid Rewards account where there are easy-to-read status bars for each goal.

There are very different methods for earning the Companion Pass than there are for earning A-List and A-List Preferred status. If the Companion Pass is your only goal, you need to act quickly. The “easy” way to do that with credit card bonuses effectively ends forever no later than Dec. 2, 2026.

This year also marks the last that many partner points count towards Companion Pass, from credit card refer-a-friend bonuses to completing hotel stays booked on the Southwest Hotels portal.

More: Last chance to earn a Southwest Companion Pass the easy way with card bonuses as high as 90,000 points

If traditional A-List or A-List Preferred status is your goal, however, here are 5 ways you can get the flights or points you might still need.

Note that beginning in 2027, Southwest will rename those tiers as part of a broader overhaul (more on that below), but that will not affect how you qualify in 2026 for 2027.

If you are only a few flights away from qualifying for Southwest status, one of the easiest ways to get to the finish line is by taking a trip or two before year’s end.

The amount of money spent doesn’t matter at all if you qualify purely by counting up the number of one-way flights flown, so book and fly the cheapest nonstop Basic fares you can find.

Use Southwest’s Low Fare Calendar to search quickly for the least expensive days to fly to various destinations. The best deals are usually midweek. Early and mid-December (between peak Thanksgiving and Christmas holiday travel) will likely offer lower prices and reduced chances of travel disruptions.

If you can’t hit a status goal by counting one-way flights and need to earn status via tier qualifying points instead, you should take the opposite approach. Instead of booking inexpensive Basic fares, book and fly Southwest’s most expensive fare option: Choice Extra.

This fare earns a whopping 14 TQPs per dollar spent in 2026. If you spend $500 on Choice Extra fares for a November or December mileage run, for example, you will add a quick 7000 TQPs to your Rapid Rewards account balance—one fifth of the way to A-List status.

Those same points are also worth about $90 when redeemed for award travel, so consider the rebate in your cost-benefit calculation.

If actually flying the airline before the year is up isn’t a realistic option, another way to earn tier qualifying points is by spending on a Southwest credit card.

The different cobranded cards earn TQPs differently in 2026. Holders of the lower annual fee (see rates and fees) are out of luck; that card doesn’t earn TQPs at all.

The higher fee cards each earn incrementally higher TQPs, as follows:

(Note, however, that all cards earn Companion Pass qualifying points at a different rate—1 point per $1 spent.)

One critical detail: TQPs earned from credit card spending only count towards 2026 status if the points post to your account before year’s end. That means it is essential to complete all spending before the closing date of your December credit card statement, meaning many travelers may only have a few weeks left.

A reminder, though: Credit card spending will count differently beginning next year for customers trying to qualify for status for 2028.

*The information for the Southwest Rapid Rewards Premier Credit Card has been collected independently by The Points Guy. The card details on this page have not been reviewed or provided by the card issuer.

If you have a card (see rates and fees) and already spend heavily on it, there is a quick and easy shortcut to Southwest A-List status (but not A-List Preferred). If you spend $75,000 on that card annually, you'll be rewarded with complimentary A-List status for the remainder of the year and the following year (activation required).

You'll also earn a $500 annual credit towards booking Southwest flights in the Chase Ultimate Rewards portal. That same spending level unlocks other perks from a variety of travel brands like Hyatt and IHG, so there are more benefits than just the Southwest ones to consider.

This method doesn’t require fussing with flight counts or TQPs or even hopping on an airplane before 2026 is up, but it’s only a viable option for a smaller subset of Southwest customers who carry the card and are capable of meeting a significant spending minimum.

Like many airlines, Southwest offers a status match promotion and challenge where you can leverage your elite status on another airline into temporary status on Southwest. If you hold status elsewhere, consider taking advantage.

The current promotion is open for registration through Dec. 30, 2026. As soon as you register, Southwest confers automatic status for a 120-day trial period. You can extend this status for another 12 months if you complete additional flights or earn additional TQPs in the promotion period.

If you plan to fly several trips on Southwest at the end of 2026 or in early 2027, this promotion might make sense. The requirements to meet the status challenge extension are substantially lower than the ones for achieving status the standard way.

Just be aware that only flights booked after registering for the status match count. If you have future Southwest travel already booked, you’ll need to cancel and rebook, potentially at higher prices.

Before committing to any of these strategies, be certain that you understand how Southwest counts Rapid Rewards points in 2026.

Southwest currently counts points three different ways. There are points redeemable only for award travel, and there are two other types that count towards status. Only tier qualifying points, earned primarily through flying or credit card spending, count towards A-List and A-List Preferred Status.

A broader collection of companion pass qualifying points (including credit card welcome bonuses) still count towards earning the Companion Pass for 2026 only.

A lot will soon change when the calendar page turns to 2027.

A-List members will become Silver, and A-List Preferred members will become Gold. Members who have earned a Companion Pass due to points activity in 2026 will continue to be able to use those benefits until the end of 2027.

If you want to earn a Companion Pass anew in 2027 or later, however, you’ll have to aim for a new status tier: Platinum. And if you want to achieve Silver or Gold in subsequent years, be aware that that benchmarks will change. The way TQPs are calculated for several Southwest fare types and for credit card spending will be different as well.

#6234. The Boeing 737 NG Still Has Years Of Flying Left, But Its Largest Operator Doesn't Want It Anymore

vesperstock | Shutterstock, Simple Flying

The symbiotic relationship between Southwest Airlines and the Boeing 737 Next Generation family has defined the very essence of low-cost domestic travel. Operating hundreds of Boeing 737-700 and Boeing 737-800 aircraft, the carrier built its legendary point-to-point network around the reliability, commonality, and rugged versatility of Boeing’s popular narrowbody workhorse. These airframes logged millions of flight hours, connecting passengers across thousands of city pairs while fostering an operational culture deeply rooted in single-type fleet efficiency.

During its September 2024 Investor Day, Southwest made a decision that stunned industry observers: a firm commitment to retire all 571 Next Generation aircraft by the end of 2031 in favor of an all-MAX fleet. This decision comes even though many of these airframes retain substantial structural and calendar life and can fly for years to come. The move is part of a profound evolution in modern airline fleet planning, where superior fuel efficiency, reduced emissions, and higher seating capacity outweigh the mechanical longevity of mature narrowbody types.

It cannot be overstated how significant Southwest's pivot is, especially given the sheer scale of the fleet involved in this generational transition. Operating 450 Next Generation aircraft consisting of 262 737-700s and 188 737-800s in active service, according to ch-aviation. Southwest is the largest operator of the type in global aviation, by some distance. These aircraft have been the fundamental building blocks of the airline's dense domestic schedules, operating multiple short-to-medium-haul legs daily with exceptional dispatch reliability.

The cornerstone of the 2031 roadmap is a dramatic rejuvenation of the carrier's asset profile, designed to bring down the average age of its operating fleet from approximately 11.5 years to just 5 years, as reported by Airline Geeks. By replacing older NG variants with new Boeing 737 MAX 8 and upcoming MAX 7 airframes, Southwest aims to modernize its operational footprint while enhancing environmental performance.

Completing a retirement campaign of this scale will not come without its challenges, especially in managing manufacturer delivery schedules, regulatory certifications, and network capacity demands. While the end-of-2031 target provides a clear strategic horizon, executive leadership has acknowledged that the exact pace remains tethered to Boeing's delivery cadence and certification timelines for smaller variant types. Consequently, while the ultimate destination is an all-MAX operational model, the winding down of the Next Generation era will be a methodical, multi-year process.

The underlying justification for moving away from the 737 Next Generation family centers entirely on modern thermodynamic efficiency and seating economics. When Southwest introduced the 737 MAX 8 into active service, manufacturer projections indicated a fuel burn reduction of approximately 14% compared to the NG airframes. In operational practice, Southwest annual reports have consistently credited fleet-wide fuel savings to the strategic integration of MAX aircraft alongside the systematic retirement of older 737-700s, turning environmental efficiency into a powerful bottom-line advantage.

A standard Southwest 737-700 accommodates 143 passengers in a single-class configuration, whereas the larger MAX 8 expands capacity to 175 passengers. This density gain allows the carrier to generate significantly higher revenue per departure on high-demand trunk routes without increasing aircraft count or slot footprint at congested airports. Ultimately, the economic performance gap between NG and MAX equipment becomes insurmountable for long-term fleet planning because of the higher passenger counts with lower fuel burn per seat.

Transitioning away from legacy NGs enables Southwest to compress its average fleet age, with benefits that may not seem obvious at first. Operating a substantially younger aircraft family slashes unscheduled maintenance events, reduces component replacement costs, and enhances schedule reliability across thousands of daily departures. The airframes of the older generation are still airworthy, but the sheer financial velocity of MAX-generation operating margins makes retaining the older fleet commercially unjustifiable.

The carrier is hyperfocused on fleet simplicity and fuel efficiency for now.

Embarking on a fleet transition of this magnitude, however, is heavily constrained by external aerospace supply chains and manufacturer delivery cadences. Southwest originally outlined an ambitious target to phase out all Next Generation aircraft by the end of 2031, but the pace of this retirement campaign is intrinsically tied to Boeing's ability to roll out new single-aisle jets from its assembly lines. Supply chain issues, regulatory scrutiny, and production-rate adjustments have repeatedly pushed carriers worldwide to recalibrate their fleet retirement horizons.

Recent operational cadences illustrate the delicate equilibrium needed between retirements and incoming deliveries. For instance, the airline retired 55 Next Generation aircraft in 2025, comprising 48 737-700s and 7 737-800s, while taking delivery of 55 new MAX 8 airframes, followed by planned schedules for roughly 66 MAX deliveries and 60 retirements in subsequent operating cycles, as per data from Cranky Flier. Annual delivery volumes fluctuate based on OEM manufacturing stability, so matching retirements one-to-one with new arrivals is a complex logistical challenge for fleet planners.

Consequently, executive leadership has adopted a pragmatic stance regarding the timeline's rigidity. Chief Financial Officer Tom Doxey noted that Southwest still maintains more than 450 Next Generation airframes that will be phased out gradually for years to come, well into the next decade, according to Aviation Week. Of course, the 2031 target is the ultimate strategic horizon, but aircraft production backlogs will likely extend the twilight of the 737 NG era beyond initial projections.

Southwest Airlines is aggressively shedding its Next Generation fleet to the point that the existing fleet seems far too outdated, though these airframes are far from obsolete and still have robust demand across the secondary global market. Regional carriers, leasing companies, and growing airlines eagerly queue for surplus 737-700 and 737-800 units, allowing Southwest to capitalize on strong secondhand asset valuations. Southwest is focused on monetizing select airframes and surplus spare engines while market conditions remain highly favorable.

The cargo sector is a particularly lucrative second life for the larger 737-800 variants. Passenger-to-freighter (P2F) conversion programs have taken on substantial inventory from major operators looking to upgrade their fleets. According to market data compiled by aviation analytics firm IBA, operators completed 265 737-800 freighter conversions between January 2020 and August 2026. These numbers show that the airframe's structural integrity and engine reliability easily outlast its primary passenger utility for carriers chasing ultra-high-density MAX efficiencies.

Consequently, the retirement of the Next Generation family is driven entirely by strategic single-fleet standardization rather than mechanical fatigue or structural exhaustion. Airframes leaving Southwest's active roster find immediate new leases on life hauling express freight or serving secondary passenger routes worldwide. It means that the 737 NG legacy will endure across global aviation networks long after Southwest completes its transition to an all-MAX operating model.

Managing a multi-year transition away from a massive fleet of aircraft takes careful coordination to maintain a consistent, competitive passenger experience on legacy airframes. The phase-out timeline extends well into the next decade, so Southwest cannot afford to let its remaining Next Generation cabins deteriorate while waiting for new deliveries. Passengers flying on older aircraft still need to enjoy a modern, comfortable onboard environment that aligns with the airline's brand standards.

Southwest has therefore invested in targeted cabin refurbishments for select 737-700s slated for extended service during the twilight of the NG era. These interior refreshes include updated seating materials, modernized cabin lighting aesthetics, and refreshed bulkheads that mirror the interior ambiance of incoming MAX jets. By revitalizing passenger touchpoints on mature airframes, the airline is ensuring there is no perceptible drop in onboard quality for travelers during the multi-year handover period.

The meticulous approach to the NG twilight highlights the operational pragmatism needed in modern fleet management. Even as executive leadership targets an all-future-generation fleet, maintaining the operational integrity and customer appeal of the existing inventory protects the carrier's reputation. The 737 Next Generation may no longer align with Southwest's long-term efficiency vision, but its final years in service are being treated with the same disciplined attention to detail that built the airline's success, and that is truly impressive.

The retirement trajectory of the 737 Next Generation fleet illustrates a profound reality in modern commercial aviation: economic obsolescence frequently arrives long before structural exhaustion. Airframes like the 737-700 and 737-800 have decades of potential calendar and cycle life, as evidenced by booming passenger-to-freighter conversions and robust secondary market demand, but the rapid gains in fuel efficiency and seating capacity offered by newer generations make holding onto older assets financially unviable for major network operators. Decarbonization goals, emissions standards, and operating margin pressures dictate that remaining useful life is superseded by the immediate return on investment delivered by modern engine and wing architectures.

Southwest is now well on its delivery-dependent path toward an all-MAX operating model over the coming decade, and once this transition is complete, the airline will likely permanently reshape North American single-aisle operations. Phasing out hundreds of airframes to establish a uniform, ultra-young fleet profile sets a new benchmark for low-cost carrier fleet strategy, showing that even a legendary aircraft family must eventually yield to the relentless march of technological progress.

#6233. All Nippon Airways (ANA) New 777 First & Business Class: Which Routes Get Them?

In 2019, Japanese Star Alliance carrier All Nippon Airways (ANA) launched an all-new first and business class product. In this post, I’d like to take an updated look at ANA’s progress with installing these new cabins, along with which routes currently consistently feature this product.

All Nippon Airways’ new first class and business class products are truly spectacular. ANA has always had incredible service, and now the airline has a hard product to match.

All Nippon Airways’ new first class, known as “The Suite,” is phenomenal. The hard product as such doesn’t look that amazing, but it’s a huge improvement over the old product. First class has eight very comfortable suites, each of which is functionally designed and private. Personally I consider this to be among the world’s best first class products, thanks largely to ANA’s top notch soft product.

All Nippon Airways’ new business class, known as “The Room,” is really what’s most revolutionary. The seats have doors and an unreal amount of personal space. I consider this to be one of the world’s best business class products, along with Qatar Airways’ Qsuites and Japan Airlines’ A350 business class.

While there are certain markets where All Nippon Airways consistently offers the new cabins, we have seen some variance. So let me share the basics of how many ANA 777s have the new cabins, how you can tell if your flight features the new cabins, and finally which routes currently feature the new cabins (though of course that’s subject to change).

All Nippon Airways has 13 Boeing 777-300ERs in its fleet. 10 of the 13 jets currently feature the new cabins, meaning that ~77% of ANA’s 777-300ERs have the new first and business class. Six of these planes have been delivered to the airline since 2019, with the new cabins, while four 777-300ERs have been reconfigured with the new cabins (these planes are 10+ years old).

Unfortunately ANA doesn’t have concrete plans to reconfigure the remaining 777-300ERs, so don’t expect this product’s footprint to grow much for the time being. ANA is expected to eventually take delivery of new 777-9s, which will likely feature this product (or something even better), though that’s still potentially years down the road.

If you want to track registration codes, the following 10 Boeing 777-300ERs feature the new cabins:

And in the interest of being thorough, here are the three Boeing 777-300ERs that feature the old cabins:

It’s obviously frustrating to have a fleet of just 13 planes, and not reconfigure three of them, especially when it has been seven years. What’s the explanation for this? Keep in mind that the 777X has been delayed by around seven years now.

My guess is that ANA had intended to reconfigure 10 planes and retire the other three, and signed contracts based on that. Then with the never-ending 777X delays, the airline decided to keep those jets around, and maybe it just proved too complicated or costly to backtrack on that. At least that’s my best guess.

You can tell whether or not your flight is scheduled to feature All Nippon Airways’ new cabins just by looking at the seat map. The easiest way to tell is to look at the business class seat map:

If you’re on ANA’s website and a flight is scheduled to be operated with the new cabins, you’ll also see the prominent display of “THE SUITE” for first class and “THE ROOM” for business class.

Another method to check without using ANA’s website is to instead go to Google Flights. Just search a business class flight on an ANA 777. When you look at the flight options, if a flight shows as having an “Individual suite,” then that’s the new business class.

Meanwhile if it shows as having a “Lie flat seat,” then that’s the old business class.

Again, it’s only select Boeing 777-300ERs that have these cabins. You won’t find these cabins on other aircraft, including 787s, A380s, etc. However:

Here are the routes that are typically currently operated by the new All Nippon Airways Boeing 777-300ERs:

In other words, as it stands, all flights to London and New York are supposed to feature the new cabins. Meanwhile flights to Chicago and San Francisco all alternate between new and old configurations, so you’ll want to check the seat map. That means there are no routes that are exclusively operated by 777s with the old cabins.

In terms of the rest of the United States route network, Houston (IAH), Los Angeles (LAX), Seattle (SEA), and Washington (IAD), are served by 787s. There’s always the chance for last minute aircraft swaps, and airlines do tweak their schedules over time.

All Nippon Airways introduced a phenomenal new first and business class in 2019, and the airline has rolled this out to ~77% of its 777-300ER fleet (though no additional retrofits have happened in the past several years).

For the current upcoming schedule, you can expect the new cabins to be offered on all flights to London and New York, as well as on select flights to Chicago and San Francisco. While you’ll always want to check the seat map for changes or aircraft swaps, that’s the current plan.

#6232. Airline Interline, Codeshare, Alliance, And Joint Venture Agreements Explained

Airline partnerships are more complex and advanced than ever before, both for better and worse. About 25 years ago the Star Alliance was formed, which was revolutionary at the time. SkyTeam and oneworld quickly joined the scene.

While they all still exist, the global alliances have definitely been deemphasized a bit in recent years. After all, with these alliances having so many members, how much can loosely affiliated airlines really have in common?

Airlines want to work with other airlines that complement them best, and this can come in many different forms. Just to give a few examples of partnerships outside of the traditional alliances:

Airlines have several different levels of cooperation, ranging from interline agreements, to codeshare agreements, to alliance membership, to joint venture agreements. In this post, I’d like to take a closer look at the differences between these agreements. Before I do so, let me add two disclaimers:

With that out of the way, let’s take a look at these four kinds of agreements.

Interline agreements are the most basic kinds of agreements you can have between airlines. An interline agreement is simply a commercial agreement between airlines to handle passengers when they’re traveling on multiple airlines on the same itinerary, and it allows an airline to issue a ticket on another airline (though not necessarily on any sort of favorable commercial terms).

This allows passengers to check their bags through to their final destination, get boarding passes all way to their destination, potentially be rebooked on another airline in the event of irregular operations, etc.

This is a basic level of cooperation, so there are airlines that have interline agreements but don’t otherwise have robust partnerships. For example, Etihad doesn’t belong to a major global alliance, but has an interline agreement with dozens of airlines, ranging from American, to Emirates, to JetBlue, to United, to Qatar Airways.

As you can see, this is a level of cooperation we even see between airlines that don’t partner with one another, and that may not even be fond of one another.

It is worth noting that in some cases airlines specifically pull out of interline agreements. For example, many years ago Delta cut its interline agreement with American. Why? At least in part it’s because Delta found that American was rebooking more passengers on Delta during irregular operations than the other way around, so the carrier no longer thought the arrangement was in its best interest.

A codeshare agreement is the next level of cooperation between airlines. This is when two airlines realize there’s value in working together, and they decide they want to place their “codes” on one another’s flights. Typically the main benefit of this is that it drums up business for the airlines that are in a codeshare agreement with one another.

Just to give an example, Alaska Airlines and Icelandair have a codeshare agreement. Icelandair flies to certain gateways in the United States, and then Alaska Airlines provides some of the “feed” for those flights in the form of codeshares.

For example, if you want to fly from Reykjavik to Los Angeles, Icelandair doesn’t operate that route. However, Icelandair flies to Portland, and then you can book a Portland to Los Angeles flight on Alaska Airlines as an Icelandair codeshare.

When you book a codeshare flight, you’ll notice that the flight number is different. So if you booked through Icelandair, your Portland to Los Angeles flight would also have an Icelandair flight number (in this case FI7696). To be clear:

With these codeshare agreements, generally neither airline is getting a huge cut for booking someone on the other airline. Most of the ticket revenue goes to the operating carrier, and often a small amount goes to the airline that sold the flight. However, the biggest advantage of this arrangement is to boost business for both airlines by increasing the number of flights that passengers have access to.

The “big three” alliances — oneworld, SkyTeam, and Star Alliance — have only developed in the past 25 years, though in the meantime many major global carriers belong to one of them. The basic way that alliances work is as follows:

I’d note that different airlines place different levels of emphasis on these alliances, even if they choose to belong to them. For example, Delta is a founding member of SkyTeam, but the airline is heavily focused on joint ventures and airlines it owns a stake in, and cares very little about the airlines it simply shares an alliance with.

If a codeshare agreement is like dating, then a joint venture is like getting married. A joint venture agreement is a massive business decision that typically requires extensive government approval. When airlines form a joint venture they coordinate pricing and schedules, and have a revenue sharing agreement.

Exactly how the revenue sharing works depends on the specific arrangement, but the idea is that two airlines are essentially acting as one under a joint venture.

Note that typically airlines form joint ventures between specific regions, which is why this is different than an outright merger. For example, American has a transatlantic joint venture with British Airways, Finnair, Iberia, and Aer Lingus, while the airline has two transpacific joint ventures, with both Japan Airlines and Qantas (the two are separate arrangements).

From the perspective of a consumer, a joint venture is both good and bad. The good news is that typically it gives you the most flight options in terms of schedules, since the airlines are operating as one. Airlines also often try to make the experience as consistent across brands as possible. The downside is that it’s like a competitor being eliminated in the market, so it could lead to higher fares as it reduces competition.

There are so many different types of agreements in the airline industry nowadays. While the exact terms vary with every partnership, I think the easiest way to sum it up is that an interline agreement is like a friendship, a codeshare agreement is like an engagement, a joint venture is like a marriage, and an alliance is like having a big family, with everyone sort of doing their own thing.

There’s a lot more to all of this, but hopefully the above provides a pretty fair and basic summary. People often misuse these terms, so I figure it’s worth recapping every so often.

If you fly United Airlines regularly, the (see rates and fees) can be a powerful way to earn more miles and reduce your out-of-pocket travel costs.

As someone who frequently flies United, I've found that the Quest hits a practical middle ground. It offers meaningful airline perks, including a $200 annual United TravelBank credit, two free checked bags and discounts on award flights, without the hefty annual fee of a premium airline card.

But with a $350 annual fee, the Quest isn't necessarily right for everyone.

Here's who I think can get the most value from the card and who might be better off with another option.

Related: I just changed my airline loyalty — here's how the United Quest Card sealed the switch

New United Quest cardholders can currently earn 500 PQP after their first purchase and 80,000 bonus miles after spending $4,000 on purchases in the first three months from account opening. Plus, you can earn another 10,000 bonus miles after adding an authorized user in the first three months from account opening.

Based on TPG's November 2026 valuations, which peg United miles at 1.2 cents apiece, the full 90,000-mile bonus is worth $1,080. That's not including the additional value of the 500 PQP, which can help you get closer to United Premier status.

While not the strongest offer we've seen in the card's history, it's still a great time to apply if you've already been considering the Quest, particularly if you have upcoming United travel planned.

There's a lot to love about the . Here's who will benefit most from having the card.

If you fly United several times per year, you'll want to take a closer look at the Quest.

That’s because many of the card’s most valuable perks are tied directly to flying United. Cardholders receive:

One of the card's strongest perks is its earning structure. The United Quest earns a strong 10 total miles per dollar spent on eligible United flights as a United MileagePlus member — that's a whopping 12% return, according to TPG's valuations (mileage earning may differ for basic economy and base option tickets).

As someone who holds Premier Silver status, I can earn a total of 12 miles per dollar spent on eligible United flights when using my Quest, which is an even better return.

But what I find especially valuable are the discounts United cardholders now receive when booking award flights. Eligible United cardholders without Premier status save at least 10% on qualifying United-operated award flights, while cardholders with Premier status save at least 15%.

I take advantage of these discounts pretty regularly. Recently, I booked two tickets from Washington, D.C.'s Dulles International Airport (IAD) to London's Heathrow Airport (LHR) for a mother-daughter trip to Europe. Thanks to my cardholder discount, each ticket cost just 34,000 miles plus $11.20 in taxes and fees, rather than 45,000 miles plus taxes and fees.

That's a savings of 11,000 miles per ticket, or 22,000 miles total, worth $264 according to TPG's valuations.

The Quest also offers two additional award flight discounts: 10,000 miles beginning with your first card anniversary and another 10,000 miles after spending $20,000 on purchases in a calendar year.

I recently used my 10,000-mile award flight discount toward a transatlantic flight from Amsterdam Airport Schiphol (AMS) to IAD. The flight would have cost 34,000 miles, but the credit brought it down to just 24,000 miles plus $112.83 in taxes and fees.

That's another $120 worth of miles saved, based on TPG's valuations.

Between the cardholder award pricing discounts and the annual award flight credits, the Quest gives me several ways to stretch my United miles further, which is why it's a card I plan to keep in my wallet long-term.

Related: United unveils huge MileagePlus shake-up, rewarding cardholders with higher earn rates

This is one of the most underrated — and potentially most valuable — perks of the United Quest Card.

The card includes two free checked bags for you and a companion on the same reservation. On domestic economy flights, United typically charges $50 ($45 if prepaid) for the first checked bag and $60 ($55 if prepaid) for the second bag.

That means you could pay up to $110 per person each way if you check two bags without a card benefit.

If you and a companion each check two bags round-trip on just one domestic flight, that could cost up to $440 total. That alone covers the Quest Card’s $350 annual fee.

Personally, I frequently fly United and regularly check two bags free thanks to my Quest Card. For travelers who often travel with a companion, don’t pack light, take longer trips or occasionally travel with bulkier items like skis or golf clubs, this benefit alone can justify holding the card year after year.

Related: These 27 credit cards can get you free checked bags on your next flight

Each account anniversary, the Quest Card provides $200 in United TravelBank cash. This credit can be used toward United-operated flights and is automatically deposited into your TravelBank account.

I recently used my $200 TravelBank credit to offset the cost of a round-trip flight from San Francisco International Airport (SFO) to IAD to visit family. The ticket originally cost $560, but my TravelBank credit brought my out-of-pocket cost down to $360.

And the TravelBank credit isn't the only statement credit available with the Quest.

Cardholders can also receive other statement credits, including:

I wouldn't go out of my way to use a credit just to justify the card's annual fee, but if you're already spending money with these merchants, they can provide some additional savings.

For me, the TravelBank credit is the easiest to use. When you subtract its $200 value from the Quest's $350 annual fee, that leaves an effective cost of $150 — assuming you can use the credit in full — before factoring in free checked bags, award flight discounts and other benefits.

If you're working toward United Premier status, the Quest Card can also help you get there.

Cardholders can earn 1 PQP for every $20 spent on purchases with the card, up to 18,000 PQP per calendar year.

Those PQP count toward United Premier status qualification, potentially helping you close the gap to your next status tier.

Plus, beginning in 2027, eligible United cardholders will receive a head start on status qualification. United will deposit PQP equivalent to 5% of the amount required for their current Premier status tier into their accounts at the start of the year. That means Premier Silver members, for example, will receive a 300-PQP boost.

I earned United Premier Silver status for the first time last year, and I've already secured it again for next year, thanks in part to the PQP boost I received at the beginning of the year and the PQP I've earned through flying and spending on my Quest.

I generally don't put much spending on the card outside of United purchases, since I have other cards that earn more flexible rewards on everyday expenses. However, I did intentionally increase my Quest spending over the past few months to earn the additional PQP I needed to secure Silver for another year.

For me, that was worth it because I regularly fly United and appreciate the benefits that come with Premier status.

Of course, I wouldn't recommend putting unnecessary purchases on a card just to earn PQP. But if you're already close to qualifying for status, the Quest can give you another way to get there.

The United Quest Card is a strong step up from the (see rates and fees) — especially for travelers who fly United more than once or twice per year.

The Explorer is a great entry-level option, with a $0 introductory annual fee for the first year (then $150) and useful perks like a free checked bag and two one-time United Club passes each year. For occasional United flyers, that may be all you need.

But if you’re booking multiple United flights annually and check bags or redeem miles, the Quest’s incremental perks can quickly outweigh the difference in annual fees and deliver stronger long-term value.

In short, the Explorer fits the occasional flyer. The Quest is designed for frequent United travelers who can maximize its recurring value.

While the is packed with benefits for United fans and frequent travelers, there are a few reasons why the card might not be the right fit. Let's take a deeper look at who the card isn't the right fit for.

While the United Quest Card has many travel-related benefits, it does not come with any lounge privileges, and you don’t get any guest passes.

If lounge access is a priority, the (see rates and fees) may be a better fit. It includes a United Club membership as part of its annual fee, which grants access for the primary cardholder and eligible guests.

And for those who don't want to pay the United Club's steep $695 annual fee, remember that the offers two guest passes annually for a much more approachable fee ($0 introductory; $150 after the first year).

That said, not everyone needs airline-specific lounge access. For example, I personally get lounge access through the Capital One Venture X Rewards Credit Card, so I don’t need the Quest Card to provide that benefit.

While the number of Capital One lounges is limited, the Venture X also includes a Priority Pass lounge membership (at participating lounges), so I rarely feel short on options.

If you also already have lounge access through another premium travel card, the lack of United Club access here may not matter.

Related: Is the United Club Card annual fee worth it?

The United Quest Card is subject to Chase’s 5/24 rule. If you’ve opened five or more personal credit cards across all issuers in the past 24 months, you’re unlikely to be approved.

If you’re currently over 5/24, you may need to wait — or consider a card from another issuer.

Related: Chase's 5/24 rule: Everything you need to know

The United Quest Card earns United MileagePlus miles. If you don’t regularly fly United — or you prefer more flexibility in how you redeem your rewards — a transferable points or miles card could be a better option.

Flexible points and miles can typically be transferred to multiple airline and hotel partners or redeemed in other ways, giving you more options.

Two strong alternatives with significantly lower annual fees include:

If you value flexibility over airline-specific perks, one of those cards may be a better long-term fit.

If you fly United multiple times per year, check bags regularly and can easily use the $200 annual TravelBank credit, the United Quest Card’s ongoing perks can quickly offset much of its $350 annual fee.

However, if you prioritize lounge access, prefer flexible points or miles over airline-specific miles or only fly United occasionally, another card — either within United’s lineup or outside of it — may be a better fit.

Ultimately, the Quest Card shines for travelers who are loyal enough to United to benefit from its airline perks but don’t need the full premium treatment of a club membership.

#6230. United Bans AI Agents From Booking Flights For Customers

In the first such move by a U.S. airline, United will ban third-party AI from parts of its digital platforms and adjust its policies to prevent access via travel agencies and aggregators.

“Sharing account credentials with personal, third-party AI assistants can expose sensitive information, and actions taken by these tools may result in unintended purchases, account changes, or use of MileagePlus miles,” the airline said in a statement.

The carrier also said AI actions could violate FAA and Department of Transportation regulations. As an example, it cited the requirement that passengers confirm in person that their bags do not contain banned items, such as explosives.

“As a result, United is taking steps to restrict access, directly within our digital platforms and indirectly via travel agencies and aggregators, to prohibit use by unauthorized, third-party personal AI agents or assistants,” the statement continued. “This work includes updates to our booking, ticketing, and distribution policies.”

United said its stance is in line with companies in the banking and retail sectors. It is now “encourag[ing] others” to consider measures “that preserve the data and security of their customers and strengthen safety.”

The airline said it will update its Digital Trust Center to clarify the new restrictions.

#6229. Plaza Premium Opening Hong Kong Arrivals Lounge… With Live Music?!

Plaza Premium will be opening an arrivals lounge soon at Hong Kong International Airport (HKG). While these facilities are always useful for a shower and breakfast after an overnight flight, it sounds like there might be a bit more planned for this arrivals lounge? I’m certainly intrigued (thanks to Sel_D for flagging this)…

Plaza Premium is expected to open an arrivals lounge at Hong Kong Airport in late November 2026. The lounge will be located on level three of Terminal 2, in the arrivals portion of the terminal, below the Airport Express platform. That means it’ll be landside.

This actually technically represents the reopening of a lounge, as the global lounge operator had such a facility until 2019. At that point it closed due to an expansion project at the airport. Once open, it will be the only arrivals lounge at the airport. Cathay Pacific used to have an arrivals lounge at its hub, but it closed in 2018, and the airline has no plans to reopen such a facility.

The exact entry requirements of the Plaza Premium arrivals lounge in Hong Kong remain to be seen, but like most Plaza Premium lounges, the expectation is that entry will be possible through select credit cards and Priority Pass, and access can also be purchased directly.

Generally we think of an arrivals lounge in terms of its functional purpose, which is to shower, have breakfast, and get some work done, before heading into the city. Many arrivals lounges are only open in the morning, since that’s when there’s the most value. That’s especially true for people who either plan to head to the office, or who are staying at a hotel, where it’s well before the published check-in time.

While it remains to be seen what exactly Plaza Premium’s facility will be like, it sounds like this will be a rather unconventional arrivals lounge, in a good way. The social media post about the new lounge describes it as “Plaza Premium Lounge – Rhythms.” It will offer a “seamless blend of dining, music, wellness, and refreshment.”

In terms of the range of amenities, we’re being promised live music, wellness experiences, refined dining, and private resting spaces. I’m sorry… live music? Like… someone performing music live? In an arrivals lounge? Fascinatingly, the pictures make it look more like an evening-oriented lounge serving cocktails and wine, for lounging around, rather than your typical arrivals lounge.

A post shared by Plaza Premium Lounge (@plazapremiumlounge)

Suffice it to say that I am very interested in what they come up with here. From a monetization standpoint, this seems kind of smart, since it could drum up more business in the afternoons and evenings, when people might not otherwise consider visiting such a facility. Then again, are people really thinking “I just got off a 15 hour flight, what I could really use is a cocktail before heading to my hotel?” Maybe they are, I suppose!

In the coming weeks, Hong Kong Airport will once again have an arrivals lounge, thanks to the opening of a facility by Plaza Premium. Arrivals lounges are usually pretty basic, and are about showers and breakfast. While we’ll see how much of this is fluff rather than actual substance, Plaza Premium is promising what sounds more like a bar vibe, with live music and cocktails. Bring it on, Plaza Premium, I can’t wait to learn more!

What do you make of this Plaza Premium concept?

#6228. Trump’s Amnesty Talk

President Donald Trump looks on as White House deputy chief of staff Stephen Miller speaks about birthright citizenship in the Oval Office at the White House in Washington, D.C., August 6, 2026.

Vice President JD Vance warned in his famous post-midterm X post that Republicans would begin advocating for amnesty in the aftermath of the election. He was right, although he didn’t mention that the president of the United States would be one of them.

In a 60 Minutes interview over the weekend, Trump said he’d like to find a deal with Democrats to regularize the legal status of good, hardworking illegal immigrants. Whenever Trump has talked in these terms in the past, or mused about increasing levels of legal immigration, his restrictionist aides have — rightly — pulled him back.

This will probably happen again, given that the president has just made the ur-immigration hawk Stephen Miller his chief of staff. Even if Trump persists, it’s hard to see how there’d be any deal in the offing with Democrats who think they won, in part, on the excesses of the president’s immigration enforcement and have a chance for a trifecta in 2028 that could roll back his immigration agenda entirely. Are they really going to make concessions on enforcement or legal immigration numbers?

There’s no doubt that the administration’s immigration regime hurt among Hispanics voters and the general electorate as well, although not nearly as much as corruption, prices, and the Iran war. With a vast illegal immigrant population in the United States and limited enforcement resources, the administration has understandably looked to self-deportation as a force multiplier. If there are high-profile apprehensions and deportations, illegal immigrants see that and decide to go home on their own. This dynamic has clearly contributed to a notable diminishment in the foreign-born population in Trump’s second term.

The political problem is that everyone else sees those apprehensions and detentions and may not like them, especially if they are needlessly combative for the sake of cable-news coverage and internet clicks. This was the approach of former DHS Secretary Kristi Noem, whose subtraction from the administration was a net addition. Border czar Tom Homan took over the immigration portfolio and has tried to avoid headlines, but enforcement has still been overwhelming based on apprehensions in public places.

What’s been missing is an emphasis on what our friends at the Center for Immigration Studies call bureaucratic or briefcase enforcement, the nuts-and-bolts work to track down, warn, and punish as necessary employers who hire illegal workers. Ideally, we’d have a national E-Verify system to instantaneously flag such workers. Still, there’s much that can be done with currently existing tools, and Homan himself favors deploying them.

If we squeeze illegal workers out of the labor market, it creates an incentive for them to leave, since so many came here looking for a job. At the same time, such largely invisible enforcement doesn’t generate occasions for demonstrations and turmoil in the streets.

Yet the president is an obstacle to adopting this tactic. He has sympathy for employers desperate for immigrant labor — since he was one himself — and influential business constituencies will balk at intense workplace enforcement. So, we have the president wildly swinging from supporting splashy actions targeting specific cities to talking about throwing in the towel.

At some point, when the illegal population is down substantially and there’s an enforcement system in place that can’t be ignored or gamed, there will be a case for amnesty for specific categories of illegal immigrants. We aren’t there yet, and we shouldn’t be thinking of giving up after one election loss. Vance implied that it was GOP quislings who would immediately turn to amnesty after the midterm drubbing, but, alas, the call is coming from inside the house.

#6227. Why Boeing 787-9 Airlines Face Different Maintenance Costs With Rolls-Royce & GE Engines

Craig Russell | Shutterstock, Simple Flying

Selecting a powerplant for a widebody fleet is one of the most consequential financial commitments an airline executive can make, locking the carrier into a multi-decade maintenance relationship that is quite tough to get out of. During the years where Boeing developed the Boeing 787 family, it made the decision to offer two distinct engine options, with the General Electric GEnx-1B and the Rolls-Royce Trent 1000. The dual-engine strategy successfully distributed supply chain risk and gave network planners purchasing leverage, but it also exposed airlines to vastly divergent operating economics and maintenance profiles.

Over the past decade, the operational histories of these two powerplants have gone on their own individual paths, driven by unexpected durability hurdles, time-on-wing variances, and costly fleet modifications. As a result, maintenance expenses can differ by millions of dollars per aircraft because of the engineering differences, repair liabilities, and long-term financial structures tied to each manufacturer.

Boeing's decision to engineer the 787 to accept two mutually exclusive engine types was rooted in lessons learned from earlier widebody programs. Offering both the General Electric GEnx-1B and the Rolls-Royce Trent 1000, Boeing wanted to show airlines that they no longer needed to be locked into a single supplier monopoly, but also to protect the airframer from production problems if one manufacturer faced factory delays. The flexibility allowed carriers to match engine performance characteristics to their specific route networks, balancing fuel burn against operating weights and thrust ratings.

The General Electric GEnx-1B is built on a twin-spool design featuring a carbon fiber composite fan and Twin Annular Pre-Swirl (TAPS) combustors, sharing operational lineage with engines powering larger Boeing aircraft. In contrast, the Rolls-Royce Trent 1000 is built on a signature three-shaft (triple-spool) configuration with intermediate-pressure stages and hollow titanium fan blades, designed exclusively for the Dreamliner family. These fundamental engineering differences meant that maintenance tooling, spare parts inventories, and overhaul procedures were entirely unique to each fleet type.

Over at the airlines, the choice initially came down to commercial inducements, leasing structures, and projected aircraft utilization. Airlines with heavy historical ties to Rolls-Royce naturally gravitated toward the Trent 1000 to maintain cross-fleet maintenance familiarity, while operators favoring General Electric chose the GEnx-1B for its established high-bypass efficiency. However, as aircraft accumulated operational flight hours, the underlying maintenance realities of each powerplant began to drift off in ways that reshaped global fleet orders.

The divergence in maintenance costs accelerated rapidly as early iterations of the Rolls-Royce Trent 1000 encountered intense, unforeseen durability hurdles. As noted by AirInsight, the powerplant's initial years in service were plagued by fatigue and corrosion issues within its intermediate-pressure turbine (IPT) blades, leading to accelerated wear and premature component failures. Although Rolls-Royce introduced the upgraded Trent 1000 TEN standard to resolve these issues, subsequent engineering evaluations showed that high-pressure turbine (HPT) blades were also wearing out significantly faster than projected design models anticipated.

What came was tough operational fallout for airlines flying Trent 1000-powered Dreamliners. It was immediate and severe, characterized by unexpected engine groundings, plummeting dispatch reliability, and soaring maintenance expenses. Major international operators such as Air New Zealand and British Airways were forced to ground aircraft for lengthy inspections and unscheduled overhauls, as reported by Aviation Week. To stick to already published flight schedules during these mandatory groundings, several affected carriers had to lease older, less fuel-efficient backup aircraft from the open market, incurring millions of dollars in supplementary operational expenses.

Airlines and their respective maintenance departments became reactionary, where engineers had to manage aggressive removal schedules and emergency component replacements well ahead of standard lifecycle intervals. While safety was rigorously maintained through constant borescope inspections and regulatory airworthiness directives, the financial toll of keeping these aircraft operational strained airline engineering budgets and disrupted long-term route planning.

While around 34% of the Dreamliners flying today have RR engines, only around 8% of the known engine option orders are for RR engines.

The mechanical difficulties encountered by the Trent 1000 triggered profound financial consequences for Rolls-Royce and caused a noticeable shift in global widebody purchasing patterns. Industry reports from Aviation Week indicate that the cumulative cost of retrofits, customer compensation, and engine modifications surpassed $3 billion for Rolls-Royce, with aviation analysts estimating that up to 500 engines across the worldwide fleet needed remediation. The massive financial liability prompted corporate restructuring and an intensified engineering focus on redesigning hot-section components to restore customer confidence.

Concurrently, the maintenance disparity heavily influenced subsequent airline procurement decisions. Fleet data compiled by Simple Flying highlights a pronounced market shift: roughly 35% of the active Dreamliner fleet operates on Trent 1000 powerplants, while 65% relies on General Electric GEnx engines. In recent sales campaigns, widebody customers overwhelmingly selected GE, ordering 677 GEnx-powered aircraft compared to just 71 for the Trent 1000. Rolls-Royce's leadership, including engineering chief Simon Burr, candidly acknowledged that the company had surrendered market share because earlier iterations of the engine were simply not sufficiently durable.

That market contraction demonstrated how crucial predictable maintenance performance is to an aircraft's commercial success. Even though airlines frequently put pen to paper on aggressive initial acquisition discounts when finalizing engine selections, the long-term cost of unreliability and frequent shop visits quickly outweighs upfront savings, making durability the primary metric for fleet evaluation.

At the heart of widebody maintenance economics is the concept of time-on-wing, or the operational duration an engine can complete commercial flights before needing a major workshop overhaul. A General Electric GEnx-1B engine stays in the wing three times longer and can frequently achieve more than 20,000 operating hours before its first major shop visit, maintaining consistent fuel efficiency and low thermal stress. This extended durability significantly reduces the frequency with which an airline must unhang heavy powerplants from the wing and transport them to certified overhaul facilities.

In contrast, the early generations of the Trent 1000 suffered from time-on-wing intervals that were a fraction of their competitor's benchmark, leading to repeated, premature shop visits. When an engine suffers an unplanned removal, the financial impact extends far beyond the repair bill. Transport logistics, spare engine leasing fees, and teardown labor mean that a single unscheduled shop visit can easily exceed $5 million in direct and indirect costs, severely impacting an airline's quarterly profitability.

Predictability is paramount for airline finance departments trying to stick to fixed operating budgets. While GEnx operators benefit from stable, linear maintenance amortization schedules, Trent 1000 operators historically faced fluctuating maintenance reserves and unexpected capital outlays to cover recurring shop visits. As a result, the reliability gap created a clear economic divide between the two subfleets, influencing how asset managers value leased 787-9 aircraft depending on which engine hangs beneath the wing.

Each engine can run into millions of dollars.

Determined to reverse its competitive disadvantage, Rolls-Royce instituted a comprehensive technical turnaround centered on its newest engine standard, the Trent 1000 XE. Designed to triple the time-on-wing performance of the older TEN variants, the XE incorporates advanced thermal barrier coatings and redesigned turbine geometry. Leadership at Rolls-Royce, including CEO Tufan Erginbilgic, noted that targeted operators could see up to six years between major shop visits, as per Reuters. Following initial certification milestones in June 2025, rollout programs are actively modernizing in-service units across global fleets through late 2027.

On the operator risk side, many Rolls-Royce airlines rely on TotalCare agreements, comprehensive power-by-the-hour maintenance contracts where the carrier pays a fixed rate per flight hour, effectively transferring the financial liability of shop visits back to the manufacturer. Rolls-Royce committed to upgrading existing Trent 1000 engines to the improved durability standard at no additional charge to airlines. However, industry analysts at Aircraft Monitor point out an enduring secondary cost: because the Trent 1000 fleet now spans multiple engineering build standards and retrofit configurations, airlines and maintenance hubs must manage complex parts inventories and tooling for varying sub-generations.

With the parts fragmentation comes an administrative and logistical overhead that can complicate line maintenance. TotalCare agreements protect airlines from direct overhaul bills, but the operational friction of supporting a mixed-standard engine fleet is still a distinct and important consideration for engineering planners comparing the streamlined configuration of the GEnx-1B ecosystem.

The divergence in maintenance costs between 787-9 aircraft powered by General Electric GEnx engines and those equipped with Rolls-Royce Trent 1000s is a case study in the unforgiving economics of modern propulsion engineering. In the beginning, the Trent 1000's early durability struggles and subsequent retrofit campaigns cost manufacturers billions and reshaped market share, but now, with ongoing technical enhancements like the XE standard, reliability is now firmly under control at Rolls-Royce.

Ultimately, choosing between these two powerplants is a choice between initial acquisition incentives and long-term lifecycle risk. The lessons learned from the Dreamliner's dual-engine experiment will continue to guide how airlines evaluate maintenance predictability across all future widebody acquisitions. Many airlines still have the 787 on order, and many others are likely to add new orders over the coming years, so it will be interesting to see if that split between both engines becomes far more even.
