#6197. Why Boeing Chose Traditional Aluminum For The 747-8's Fuselage When Airbus Used Hybrid Material On The A380

Wikimedia Commons, ajuangon | Shutterstock, Simple Flying

Airbus built the A380 as a completely clean-sheet, brand-new design, whereas Boeing designed the 747-8 as an evolution of its existing 747-400 platform. The European planemaker's design enabled the maker to incorporate unproven, cutting-edge hybrid materials into a newly designed factory infrastructure; Boeing chose traditional aluminum for the 747-8's fuselage to maintain production compatibility, minimize development costs, and speed up its time-to-market.

Boeing reused the same manufacturing jigs, tools, and fuselage cross-section geometry as older 747 models for its final iteration of the iconic jumbo jet. Changing the primary material to a hybrid or composite would have forced Boeing to completely redesign the production line. Opting for traditional aluminum ensured production continuity and structural designs, adhering to proven standards and avoiding billions of dollars in infrastructure costs.

For a niche, low-volume superjumbo market, Boeing could not financially justify building a brand-new factory line. This choice reflects the challenges faced when modifying an existing aircraft's design, which limits flexibility and necessitates adherence to historical practices. Boeing chose to spend its engineering and material budget where it mattered most, which was the wings. The 747-8 features advanced alloys and carbon-fiber composites, applying engineering breakthroughs borrowed from the 787 Dreamliner.

While carbon fiber composites (CFRP) would have provided even higher weight savings, aluminum avoided billions in infrastructure costs that would have come with a 747-8 made with advanced hybrid materials. CFRP and other composites require billions of dollars in specialized molds, tape-laying robotics, and colossal autoclaves. Because the superjumbo market for the 747-8 was projected to be a low-volume, niche segment, Boeing could justify the manufacturing infrastructure costs.

Airbus was also forced to curtail much of its composite use in the A380 due to limited market demand for the superjumbo. Thus, the A380 uses Glass Laminate Reinforced Aluminum (GLARE) selectively, applying roughly 5,382 square feet (500 square meters) of it strictly to the upper shell of the front and rear fuselage sections. Airbus chose this layout because the top of a double-decker passenger cabin is under constant high-tensile stress from internal pressurization.

Over thousands of flights, this pressure cycles up and down, causing traditional aluminum to form tiny microscopic cracks. Boeing encountered complications when using new aluminum-lithium alloys, which cracked during production, leading to additional weight and financial repercussions. Meanwhile, the internal glass-fiber layers inside GLARE act as microscopic firewalls. If a fatigue crack forms in the aluminum layer, it hits the glass fibers and stops dead, allowing Airbus to shave thousands of pounds off the upper fuselage weight while making the cabin safer.

How carriers around the world are filling the jumbo-sized void left by an icon of aviation.

During the development of the A380 and the 747-8, engineers advanced third-generation aluminum-lithium (Al-Li) extrusions for internal fuselage structures such as stringers, floor beams, and seat tracks. Lithium is the lightest metallic element, and adding it to aluminum reduces density while significantly increasing stiffness, offering an attractive way to shed weight without switching to CFRP.

The Airbus A380 is a massive, full double-decker leviathan built with an optimized cabin volume, whereas the Boeing 747-8 is a sleek, stretched evolution of a classic platform designed with a tighter cross-section and a wing footprint optimized for speed over sheer bulk. Despite this massive difference in physical scale, where the Airbus operates with vastly more structural dead weight, both engineering teams smashed into the exact same metallurgical and financial barriers when trying to step into next-generation materials.

Early implementation of Al-Li ran into severe structural issues, specifically micro-cracking and stress corrosion cracking along the grain boundaries created during the extrusion process. The table below illustrates the scale of the massive jets:

The physical realities of shear loads and bending stresses around major openings forced both companies to abandon advanced materials in high-stress zones, requiring Airbus to strip GLARE off the aircraft belly to prevent compression buckling and forcing Boeing to keep traditional monolithic aluminum around its massive cargo doors to endure industrial freight operations.

Simultaneously, the manufacturing process of GLARE necessitated advanced factory equipment. Fokker employed a technique of rolling thin aluminum sheets over glass fiber layers, using a high-capacity autoclave for curing. This innovative assembly method permitted the creation of larger panels than traditional processes would normally allow, as the glass fiber effectively bridges the seams between metal layers.

Mothballed giants are coming back online.

Early assembly work on the first 747-8 to commence flight testing, RC501, revealed significant metallurgical issues, with parts exhibiting thermal warping, low fracture toughness, and stress corrosion cracking. The cracking crisis forced engineers to immediately abandon or pull back on advanced lightweight extrusions and execute a quick reversion to heavier, conventional aerospace alloys like standard aluminum.

In an identical parallel, the internal wing ribs and brackets of the Airbus A380 experienced similar structural fracturing under assembly stress, prompting Airbus to spend hundreds of millions of dollars retrofitting early-production aircraft with standard, heavier aluminum components to ensure structural safety. Meanwhile, cargo carriers saw the complex maintenance of a material like GLARE as a liability and potential failure point.

December 19, 2000 (Launched as the A3XX program)

November 14, 2005 (Launched as the 747 Advanced)

November 12, 2009 (Freighter) / February 13, 2011 (Passenger)

February 8, 2010 (Freighter) / March 20, 2011 (Passenger)

October 15, 2007 (Delivered to Singapore Airlines)

October 12, 2011 (Freighter to Cargolux) / May 5, 2012 (Passenger to Lufthansa)

October 12, 2011 (Freighter) / June 1, 2012 (Passenger)

December 16, 2021 (Final delivery made to Emirates)

January 31, 2023 (Final delivery made to Atlas Air)

Boeing chose to stick entirely with aluminum for the 747-8 fuselage to keep operations simple, 'bulletproof,' and easy to patch anywhere in the world. Even Airbus followed this approach when configuring the lower fuselage sections of the A380 where cargo doors are located. In places where heavy bending stresses occur, GLARE and other composites were entirely removed in favor of advanced monolithic aluminum alloys to resist buckling and shear loads.

Cargo flats are getting older, and the end is getting further out of sight. With delays more common than ever, when will cargo operators modernize?

The historical collaboration between Fokker Aerostructures and the development of the Airbus A380 and Boeing 747-8 helps illustrate the ongoing challenge of weight reduction in both programs. Fokker, in the latter half of the 20th century, advanced the science of structural metal bonding by replacing mechanical riveting with specialized adhesive techniques. This technique evenly distributed internal stresses across aerospace-grade aluminum layers, creating exceptionally fatigue-resistant structures.

By the late 1980s, Fokker enhanced this technology through a research partnership with the Delft University of Technology to develop GLARE, a hybrid material featuring ultra-thin sheets of glass-fiber epoxy sandwiched between aluminum layers. Airbus utilized this lightweight laminate across the massive upper fuselage of the A380 to absorb high-altitude pressurization loads and shed thousands of pounds of empty weight. In contrast, the Boeing 747-8 could not accommodate Fokker's advanced material because the program relied strictly on a derivative design strategy that reused legacy tooling.

Integrating GLARE into the 747-8 supply chain would have required Boeing to abandon its existing assembly lines and invest billions in specialized cleanrooms and autoclave infrastructure, destroying the financial logic of the program. Ultimately, both manufacturers had to retreat to conventional aluminum alloys in high-stress zones, reaffirming Fokker’s early technical warnings that lightweight hybrid materials remain structurally limited when subjected to severe, multi-axial operating forces.

The aircraft will be replaced by other highly capable, but smaller, widebodies.

The commercial decline of the quadjet era is perfectly epitomized by the severe structural and financial challenges that plagued the 747-8. Launched in 2005 as the 747 Advanced, the program aimed to merge the next-generation cockpit and engine technologies of the 787. Initial production models suffered from drastic weight growth and excessive fuel burn, prompting launch customer Cargolux to flatly reject its first deliveries in late 2011 until steep financial compensations and emergency engine upgrades were secured.

The passenger version, introduced by Lufthansa in 2012, also struggled with engineering issues, including emissions mandates that compromised its performance. By 2023, only 155 units were produced, largely freighters, highlighting a market shift towards ​​​​​​​efficient twinjet designs like the 787 and A350. When the final 747-8 Freighter rolled off the line and was delivered to Atlas Air on January 31, 2023, it brought a definitive end to a historic 54-year production span, coming just over a year after Airbus closed its own A380 assembly line in December 2021.

JSX is bringing its popular semi-private flights to Beantown.

The boutique air carrier plans to begin flying from Boston this winter, JSX said this week. The company's service will be based out of the nearby Laurence G. Hanscom Field (BED) in the town of Bedford, Massachusetts.

The Boston service will launch with a route to New York City on Feb. 8, followed by flights to Miami-Opa Locka Executive Airport (OPF) in Florida beginning on Feb. 11.

More: JSX eyes more turboprops and new mountain routes after strong passenger response

JSX will operate four daily flights between Boston and New York from Monday through Friday, with two flights on Saturday and three on Sunday. The Miami service will run once per day five times a week: Monday, Thursday, Friday, Saturday and Sunday.

Notably, JSX did not specify which New York airport would host the Boston flights. A spokesperson did not immediately answer TPG’s request for further details. JSX typically flies to New York’s Teterboro Airport (TEB) and Westchester County Airport (HPN), although various restrictions set by the Port Authority of New York and New Jersey mean that JSX cannot publicly promote TEB as a destination.

Because of those restrictions, anyone looking to fly to or from New York has to sign up for the free Club JSX program, which offers rewards and has no minimum spending or flying requirements. Passengers can also earn United MileagePlus miles under a partnership between the two companies.

The carrier will use its Embraer E145 aircraft on both routes, which can seat up to 30 passengers in a 1-1 configuration. Fares start at $199 one-way between Boston and New York, with one-way flights between Boston and Miami starting at $599.

Club JSX: Earn rewards and fly in comfort with JSX’s new loyalty program

“Greater Boston represents an exciting new chapter for JSX, marking our first entry into Massachusetts and an important milestone in the continued expansion of our East Coast network,” JSX CEO Alex Wilcox said in a statement.

“As one of the nation's leading centers for business, innovation, and higher education, Greater Boston is a natural fit for our unique approach to flying,” he added.

JSX operates as a “hop-on charter” service, which essentially operates private charter flights that anyone can buy a seat on. It means that JSX flights operate more like private flights than commercial, using posh private Fixed-Base Operators (FBOs) instead of public airport terminals and allowing passengers to venture from curb to seat in just 20 minutes.

The flight experience itself is equally luxurious with no middle seats, lots of legroom, Starlink Wi-Fi, complimentary snacks and drinks and checked luggage that’s returned right at the side of the plane. Overall, the service pitches the idea of private jet convenience for a fraction of the cost.

The public charter service — which does not bill itself as an “airline,” due to different regulations between charter carriers and public airlines — operates out of 29 airports across the U.S. and Mexico. Although private jet passengers typically bypass TSA screening, JSX implemented a more thorough in-house screening process in 2025 to address security concerns.

Still, the process is remarkably quicker than going through the public terminal, making JSX an appealing option for those looking to skip the hassle of a regular flight.

JSX's flights from Boston are already on sale, with service scheduled to start in February.

With the entry to New England, JSX adds its 29th city, and brings its own entry to the competitive business of moving premium travelers between Boston and New York.

#6195. JetBlue’s New First Class Is Missing A Cabin Divider… But Why?!?

In the coming weeks, JetBlue will be introducing a domestic first class product for the first time, which will be known as BlueFirst. This is an exciting and long overdue development, and I trust it will help JetBlue’s revenue performance, especially given how efficiently planes are being reconfigured (by reducing legroom in economy).

The first aircraft has now been retrofitted with the new cabins, and it appears that JetBlue had a media day today for this showing off both the new hard and soft product. We already largely knew what to expect, but what stands out to me is the one thing that’s missing, which I really can’t make sense of.

I don’t want to bury the lede here, so let me get right to it — on planes with BlueFirst, JetBlue won’t have any sort of a cabin divider between first class and the rest of the cabin. It’s not just that there isn’t a curtain, but there’s not even a divider hanging from the overhead bins.

JetBlue unveiled its new domestic first-class seats Wednesday as more of the country’s carriers bet on the premium travel boom to make them profitable again.Read more: https://t.co/5o3k2Ru5R9 pic.twitter.com/1BTcLVOr7s

I guess this also explains the very creative angles of the renderings that have been released up until now, which clearly try to avoid highlighting this reality.

I really can’t make sense of this decision. I know we no longer live in an era where there are real, full bulkheads between cabins, since that’s not efficient. But just installing a small, flimsy divider, along with a curtain, costs very little, doesn’t weigh a lot, etc.

To be clear, this isn’t about “oh, I don’t want to be seen by anyone.” Instead, it’s about managing traffic to and from the forward lavatory. At US airlines, the most common policy is that on domestic flights, you can use any lavatory onboard the aircraft, even in a different cabin. There are some exceptions, including for JetBlue Mint, but that’s also easier to enforce thanks to how the A321 is configured, with a lavatory behind Mint, in front of economy.

I’m not sure if JetBlue intends to reserve the forward lavatory for BlueFirst passengers, but either way, you can expect there will be a steady stream of passengers lining up to use the forward lavatory. So it’s not even about potentially not having a dedicated lavatory, but instead it’s about just constantly having people standing in the aisle right by your seat. This will also make the life of the first class flight attendant more difficult.

Take Aer Lingus AerSpace, for example, which is Aer Lingus’ premium product on short haul flights in Europe. It’s simply the first row of seats with blocked middles, and no divider between that and the rest of the plane. The problem is that if you’re seated in the aisle in AerSpace, you basically just have someone’s butt in your face the entire flight. You’re almost better off not booking the product, just to avoid that.

Anyway, I can’t really make sense of this decision, so I’d be fascinated to know what the logic was. There’s not another US airline with first class that has no separation between first class and economy. Spirit’s “Big Front Seat” didn’t have any divider, but that also wasn’t first class — it was just an, ummm, big front seat.

Similarly, Breeze Airways’ “Nicest” product also doesn’t have a divider, but it’s also not a separate cabin.

CNBC’s Phil Le Beau was onboard JetBlue’s first BlueFirst A320 with CEO Joanna Geraghty. I like Le Beau, but this interview is also the perfect example of why I just don’t really value interviewing airline executives in a traditional sense.

Le Beau asked Geraghty a good question — “did you wait too long to add a first class?” If we are being honest, there’s only one correct answer, which is OF COURSE. Like, unarguably, JetBlue was at least years late, if not a decade late, to introducing first class. That’s not even Geraghty’s fault, it’s that previous CEO Robin Hayes was perhaps one of the least focused CEOs the US airline industry has ever seen.

Geraghty’s answer, though, was “I don’t think we’ve waited too long, we’ve had Mint for a very long time, it just takes time with some of these products to roll them out.” I get it — nobody wants to be, like “we screwed up and waited too long, but I mainly blame the guy before me.”

Seriously, though, if she really doesn’t think JetBlue waited too long to commit to introducing first class, then I’d question how observant the executive team has been of the industry. I mean, Frontier announced it would introduce first class before JetBlue, which should tell you all you need to know. Oh, and Frontier will even have divider, even if it doesn’t have recline, food, or drinks!

Also, the below screen grab from the interview gave me a chuckle…

JetBlue’s BlueFirst class is entering service soon, which is exciting. I’m a huge fan of JetBlue, and I think historically they’ve done a great job with both their hard and soft product, and have great attention to detail. So I’m just a bit puzzled as to how they came to the conclusion that there was no need to introduce a cabin divider between first class and economy.

JetBlue will be the first airline in the US with first class to not have any sort of a cabin divider, and I can’t make sense of that.

What do you make of JetBlue’s odd cabin divider decision?

#6193. United Airlines Bans “AI Agents,” Claims It’s To “Protect Customers”

United Airlines has just banned travelers from using “AI Agents” to book or service tickets (thanks to TravelinWilly for flagging this). That’s an interesting stance for United, easily the country’s most tech savvy airline, to take. So what’s actually going on here?

United Airlines has today updated its contract of carriage, which are the terms that passengers have to agree to when they book a ticket. In the section about prohibited practices at the airline, the carrier added the following:

The use of AI Agents to make, modify or service a Ticket, and/or to purchase any service or product.

The “AI Agents” term is defined by United as follows:

AI Agent means any software or service, including but not limited to an AI assistant, AI agent or AI-enabled browser that takes autonomous or semi-autonomous action, whether or not Passenger or another individual supervises or approves its actions, to discover, search for, book, purchase, ticket, service or manage any product or service offered by or through United, including flights, seats, upgrades, ancillary products and partner products, on behalf of or at the instruction of Passenger or other individual. AI Agents include but are not limited to: (i) AI assistants built into social media, messaging, search or other consumer platforms; (ii) AI-enabled browsers and standalone AI agents; and (iii) any third-party AI assistant that accesses United through a tool, application or connection provided by a travel agency or other intermediary.

United even put out a press release about this change, claiming that it’s making the change to “protect” customers. Here’s part of the explanation:

Sharing account credentials with personal, third-party, AI assistants can expose sensitive information, and actions taken by these tools may result in unintended purchases, account changes, or use of MileagePlus miles. Plus, these automated AI actions have the potential to violate FAA and DOT regulations – as an example, flight check-in requires human acknowledgment that bags do not contain banned substances like explosives.

United claims it’s taking steps to restrict this kind of access, both directly within its digital platforms, and indirectly via travel agencies and aggregators, to prohibit use by unauthorized, third party personal AI agents or assistants.

It goes without saying that use of AI is becoming exponentially more popular in recent times, and is a force to be reckoned with. It’s anyone’s guess just how far it goes, in terms of how much the average person uses it in their everyday life.

There are certainly aspects of AI that are incredibly annoying, whether you look at it as an individual or a business. Admittedly I’m biased, but I’m so tired of feeling like half of what I’m reading online (whether on social media or websites) is written by a computer and not a human. It even extends to things like TripAdvisor reviews.

It’s also frustrating how many people write 30 paragraph emails nowadays, which are clearly 90% AI. I don’t really understand how that makes anyone’s life better. As far as I’m concerned, just give me the bullet points you fed your AI buddy, and we’ll all be better off for it. Anyway, rant over, back to United…

I suspect United’s real motive here is that it doesn’t want AI automatically being able to track and reprice flights (and then issue vouchers for passengers), or being able to too closely compare overall value on different airlines. For that matter, it probably just doesn’t want a third party getting that much data on the airline, not to mention that all of this can take a considerable toll on servers, if this scales.

But here’s what I find most interesting — the way this rule is written strikes me as being incredibly broad, no? Not to repeat the quote again, but this is the part I’m referencing, in particular:

AI Agent means any software or service, including but not limited to an AI assistant, AI agent or AI-enabled browser that takes autonomous or semi-autonomous action, whether or not Passenger or another individual supervises or approves its actions, to discover, search for, book, purchase, ticket, service or manage any product or service offered by or through United, including flights, seats, upgrades, ancillary products and partner products, on behalf of or at the instruction of Passenger or other individual.

Any software that automatically “discovers” or searches for any product or service offered by United would include all award search tools (along with all kinds of other businesses), no? Is that actually the intent here, or does United just plan to selectively enforce rules? We did see Air Canada engage in a battle over this a few years back, so is United planning something similar?

United Airlines has today updated its rules to ban “AI Agents,” and the airline even put out a press release about it. The company claims it’s making this change to protect customers and their accounts, as AI bots could have unintended consequences.

Many people are understandably skeptical of that explanation, as I imagine the airline also wants to ban these kinds of things to help people reprice tickets, get better fares, etc. For that matter, based on how broadly the definition is written, it seems that even things like award search engines would be banned.

I think this is likely a combination of pricing data protection (there are sites today that have a lot of access but there are limits to how it can be leveraged individually, whereas you could have your own agent do data scrapes specific to flights you want to book), and getting ahead of the potential for thousands of individual agents scraping airline websites and either causing stability issues or running up their hosting costs. They also want to protect their own ability to create their own agents that have unique access to their data (and potentially charging for that). Amazon has done the same thing - and went as far as to limit the descriptions and details they provide in order emails now so Google can't scrape the data from Gmail accounts.

It's pretty clear that when an AI agent books a ticket for the user, United is not liable for mistake. What's more interesting, though, is if there's a third party service like cheapflights.ai or something that the user can pay to book them a good flight. If the website screws up, is the user or cheapflights.ai liable? More abstractly, in an agentic SaaS scenario, does the agent owner or the agent operator bear liability?

AI agents would have a terrible look to book ratio, which will drive up costs for the airline. This has been around for travel agents for years. If we shop too much but book to little, we'll get reprimanded. Since that can't be done with bots, they have to be stopped somehow from shopping around too much. A human can perform only a limited number of searches at a time, whereas bots theoretically could search indefinitely. That would bring server and CRS costs go through the roof.

This seems pretty clear to stop an AI agent that would auto rebook the flight as it gets cheaper.

Horse has bolted. UA might as well get used to the flood and find a way to integrate such searches into its business. we are quickly heading to a future where your personal bot will be shopping from the merchants' bots.

#6191. Singapore Airlines Reconsiders New Business Class Seat Design After Backlash

Last week, Singapore Airlines unveiled all-new cabins, with the most exciting developments being a new first class and new business class. The new cabins look great (nothing revolutionary, but a huge improvement), with one exception — the new business class seat colors. Not only do they look cheap, but they just seem completely mismatched to the rest of the cabin.

While the airline vehemently defended the color choices for several days, it seems that they’re at least now reconsidering it, though it remains to be seen if it’s too late to make a change…

On Wednesday, November 11, 2026, Singapore Airlines CEO Goh Choon Phong had a town hall with employees, as reported by The Business Times. During this, he was asked about the negative feedback the airline has received about the new business class seat design.

In response to this, he reportedly said “we’ll look at it, we’ll see what’s feasible.” So that signals some willingness to make changes, though admittedly with how far out seats are ordered, that’s not necessarily so straightforward, so I wouldn’t count on anything happening. He did, however, emphasize that customers will come to like the seats after experiencing its comforts for themselves.

At the town hall, Singapore Airlines Chief Commercial Officer Lee Lik Hsin said this was a good learning point for the airline, but indicated that he hopes customers will mind the colors less after experiencing the seats. He also reportedly said “I suppose, you know, it’s the 80-20 rule, you can’t please them all.”

At the time of launch, Singapore Airlines VP of Product Experience, Ong Wah Li, explained the new design was in response to customer feedback, and described it as “modern, fresh, yet elegant and refined, that’s suited to business travel.”

BMW Designworks was behind the design of the cabin, and CEO Julia de Bono defended the color choices at the launch event, describing them as “more refreshing and more progressive.” As she viewed it, “what I see when I look at it, it’s definitely like a nice suit, with the white and the metal really popping out, you know, it’s more like a suit with a sneaker, so a bit more modern and fresh.”

To state the obvious, the trim and finishes on a new business class seat are hardly the most pressing issues facing the world. However, Singapore Airlines prides itself in being perhaps the most detail oriented airline in the world, because management has an obsessive attention to even the smallest things.

So I can’t help but be a bit confused by all of this:

It also just feels to me like the mandate for the design of this product was off, as shared by the CEO of BMW Designworks. Premium travel demand is through the roof, and a lot of people in premium cabins aren’t traveling for business. For that matter, these cabins will be operating the world’s longest flights, so this isn’t a case of a business traveler hopping on a plane in a suit, and going straight to a meeting (at least that doesn’t make up a meaningful percentage of the traffic here).

Is “suit with a sneaker” really the vibe you want to go for with a new business class product that’s on an airline that’s known for its incredible warmth? It’s almost like the airline views warmth and modernity as being at odds with one another, which I don’t at all agree with.

For example, reader Sam asked AI to take the new seat, but preserve the old color concept, and below is what it spit out.

That looks so much more on brand for Singapore Airlines than what the airline actually arrived at.

I would’ve loved to be a fly on the wall when this design was finalized. Was everyone immediately onboard with this, and thought it looked great? Or was there some skepticism, but someone said “trust me, people will love this, this is what a modern cabin looks like?”

I just don’t understand how you can commit to investing in a project that costs billions of dollars, reportedly get feedback from hundreds of customers, and still end up so far off the pulse of public sentiment.

Last week, Singapore Airlines unveiled its new cabins, which is an exciting development. Everything looked pretty great, except the new business class seat finishes, which seem terribly mismatched to the brand. The airline claimed it wanted something modern and progressive, but I’m not sure “suit with sneakers” is really the aesthetic that the public wanted (or that the chosen finishes actually reflect that).

Singapore Airlines leadership claims it’s now looking into possibly updating finishes, but I wouldn’t count on anything coming of that, given how far along this is.

What do you make of this Singapore Airlines business class design fiasco? And I’m still waiting for someone to please tell me that they love the design, and think it’s great!

#6190. The Rise of the Rosé States

A rosé state’s political disposition is recognizably Republican, but that disposition is conditional on a normie GOP.

Karno Muji Saputra/Getty Images, NR Illustration

When Ted Cruz was up for reelection in Texas in 2024 (and Trump hadn’t yet been swept back into power), I had a conversation with a political operative who had just gotten back from running a mock debate with him. We talked about Cruz and John Cornyn and what kind of Republican each was, and how they would fare in a world where Trump completed his comeback.

I spitballed an idea that had been kicking around in my head for a time: that Texas wasn’t as red as everybody thought, or at least not as uniformly MAGA; that it was still much closer to the state George W. Bush took over from outgoing Governor Ann Richards in 1995; and that election results had largely masked an underlying political disposition that was a quite light shade of red. Given that reality, I said, Cornyn was a better indication of where Texas voters were than Cruz.

Karno Muji Saputra/Getty Images, NR Illustration

While it would be a dream to get to every new hotel within days of opening to be among the first to experience special properties around the world, the reality is, that’s not always possible. When it is, though, you can bet we jump on the opportunity. Especially when it’s a flagship new points hotel.

That’s how I ended up staying at the gorgeous new Waldorf Astoria Kuala Lumpur within a week of its opening on Oct. 30, 2026. To be clear, I understood that not all the hotel’s restaurants would be open, nor would its spa, so this is not a full review, rather a first glimpse at what’s sure to be a favorite Hilton points redemption option soon.

Although it’s the Malaysian capital’s newest hotel, the Waldorf Astoria actually occupies the site of the storied former Hotel Istana in the heart of city’s Golden Triangle district — so called because it is the capital’s main financial and shopping district, with luxury megamalls galore — which means it’s centrally located, but tucked onto a quiet stretch of Jalan Raja Chulan.

Because of that, the hotel feels secluded and quiet, but plugged into the rest of the city, and easily accessible to most of the activities international visitors are likely to seek out while in town.

The hotel feels like a destination unto itself, too, though, thanks to its palatial suites (no mere rooms here) and an impressive slate of bars and restaurants, including outposts from celebrity chef Jean-Georges Vongerichten and Bangkok-based Garima Arora. The hotel will also be home to Malaysia’s first and only La Prairie spa, and the outdoor pool is the perfect place to while away a tropical afternoon.

Here’s what else you should plan to do during your stay at the new Waldorf Astoria Kuala Lumpur.

During my stay, only a fraction of the accommodations were ready for guests, but the hotel should be at full strength soon. There are no rooms here, just suites, which start at an impressive 80 square meters (861 square feet).

Deboss Collective is behind the decor, and sought inspiration from traditional Malay construction and crafts, incorporating lots of natural stone and timber, woven textiles and wooden furnishings that feel like contemporary urban updates to what you might find in a traditional rumah kampung, or village house.

To wit, there are huge windows overlooking the hotel grounds and the city skyline, letting in plenty of natural light. The carpet patterns and hardwood are meant to evoke traditional Malaysian marquetry while colorful accent walls call to mind vibrant Peranakan shophouses you can still find in parts of the city.

My suite’s footprint was enormous, with a huge, welcoming living area that included a 65-inch flatscreen television, a breakfast table which could double as a workdesk thanks to a panel of plugs, a rounded sofa and armchair and a low-slung wooden chair that blended colonial and midcentury influences.

In the separate bedroom, a king-size bed was dressed with crisp white sheets embroidered with a “WA,” just in case you forgot where you were. To either side were walls with a terete theme hearkening to the bamboo stalks that grow in gardens around the city. Another 55-inch flatscreen hung on the wall in there.

The bathroom was mostly white marble, including geometric floor tiling, but the countertops were a handsome darker hue. Anchoring the entire space was an elliptical standalone tub with a scalloped shell, while a water closet and separate walk-in shower stood close by. To lend a sense of place, the bath products are from Jo Malone’s Jo Loves line and scented with citrusy-fresh pomelo, which is a staple in Malaysian cuisine.

Considering this was a standard category room, it felt positively palatial, with a huge amount of real estate that provided a variety of distinct spaces to enjoy within the suite at different times.

The Waldorf Astoria isn’t the biggest hotel in town, but it fields an outsize roster of restaurants that should be a draw for guests and Kuala Lumpur locals alike.

You can’t call your hotel a Waldorf Astoria if it doesn’t have a version of Peacock Alley, the famous lobby lounge from the New York City original. The one here sits smack dab at the hotel entrance and has soaring ceilings, sculptural marble columns, dramatic overhead chandeliers and a variety of seating vignettes that feel homey yet upscale.

The all-day menu offers items like chicken skewers with lemongrass and coriander ($10.50), a Waldorf salad ($14.50), a smash burger ($22) and Malaysian nasi goreng ($17) among other options.

Named after the previous hotel to occupy this spot, Istana is the hotel’s all-day dining restaurant and is adjacent to the lobby. Breakfast includes an extensive buffet and both Western and Asian dishes. For lunch and dinner, you’ll find specialties like spiced Borneo chicken wings with a honey glaze ($10.50), chargrilled red snapper with wild ginger chili sambal ($23.75) and fresh fiddlehead ferns from the Cameron Highlands sauteed in coconut milk with tongue-torching bird’s eye chili ($8.75).

If you’re up for it, the durian dessert with coconut cream and a palm sugar compote and served with toasted buttery buns is a rich way to end the evening ($12).

This is Vongerichten’s farm-to-table concept, so you’ll find a menu focused on seasonal fruits and vegetables. The signature eggplant dip is smoky and smooth with tangy coconut yogurt and tomato chutney served with fluffy pita ($9.75). There are also tartines like a king crab crostini with tart lemon aioli and dill ($16.50), various pizzas and pastas, and an array of plant-based dishes including pistachio-crusted broccoli with hazelnut vinaigrette ($14.50).

At the entrance to ABC Kitchens KL, there is a bright, casual area with a cocktail bar and small plates.

Jean-Georges Vongerichten has a longstanding relationship with the Waldorf Astoria brand, so it should be no surprise that the signature restaurant here is a French-Malaysian fine-dining fusion restaurant courtesy of the chef. It is only open for dinner Tuesday-Saturday. I did not have the opportunity to dine here, but the menu features an entire caviar section, starters like diver scallops with caramelized cauliflower and caper-raisin emulsion ($29.50) and spice-charred duck breast with roasted cabbage and chili-lime broth ($39.50).

It was not yet open during my stay, but Yaari will be the hotel’s sophisticated Indian restaurant and will only be open for dinner from Wednesday-Sunday. The chef is Garima Arora, whose Bangkok restaurant, Gaa, holds two Michelin stars.

Located on the fourth floor, Coda feels like a swanky hideaway for those in the know. Glossy dark stone surfaces and emerald-green velvet chairs and banquettes give the space a swanky vibe, as does the menu of libations inspired by various vinyl albums, one of which will likely be spinning on the record player during your visit.

Even the classics get a Malaysian twist, like an old fashioned crafted with jerky-like beef bak kwa-washed Michter’s bourbon, cardamom, clove and cascara distillate and mandarin-infused jaggery for a sweet finish ($20.50).

Here are some of the Waldorf Astoria Kuala Lumpur’s other amenities:

Nightly rates at the Waldorf Astoria Kuala Lumpur start at around $520 or 100,000 Hilton Honors points.

The Waldorf Astoria Kuala Lumpur is part of  American Express Fine Hotels + Resorts, so if you have or , you can make a booking through amextravel.com and receive perks like availability-based upgrades, up to a $100 credit to use on-property during your stay for things like drinks or meals, complimentary daily breakfast for two and guaranteed 4 p.m. late checkout.

Both cards now offer a biannual $300 (up to $600 per calendar year) statement credit on prepaid stays at Amex Fine Hotels + Resorts, so you could save $300 on a reservation at the hotel if you are able to take advantage of one of these cards’ credits. Just note that this benefit is changing in 2027 and will require cardholders to book two nights or more to take advantage of the credit.

Related: Our favorite American Express Fine Hotels + Resorts around the world

All public areas at the Waldorf Astoria Kuala Lumpur are wheelchair-accessible thanks to elevators (with wheelchair-height buttons), ramps and wide pathways. The hotel has accessible rooms in the King Urban Deluxe category. These accommodations feature audio and visual alarms, an automatic door closer, and wheelchair-height door viewer.

The Waldorf Astoria Kuala Lumpur is an exciting new points option in the Malaysian capital, and one with plenty of award availability. While 100,000 points is a lot to pay, considering the sheer size of the suites here and the relatively high (for Kuala Lumpur) price point, it might be well worth it. Once the hotel’s restaurants and spa are all open and operational, this should become one of the city’s most popular luxury hotels.

#6187. The Real Reason Why Boeing Is Building The F-47 Stealth Fighter And Not Lockheed

When the United States Air Force announced in March 2025 that Boeing would build its next-generation air-superiority fighter, the stealthy, sixth-generation F-47, the decision sent shockwaves through the defense and aviation communities. For decades, Lockheed Martin has been the undisputed champion of American stealth design, producing icons like the F-22 Raptor and F-35 Lightning II.

Boeing’s victory marks a dramatic turning point not only for the company’s future, but for how the US plans to maintain air dominance in the decades ahead. This was no routine contract award. The F-47 program is the centerpiece of the Next Generation Air Dominance initiative, the most ambitious combat-aircraft project since the 1980s.

Its goal is to ensure US air superiority into the 2030s and beyond, combining a crewed fighter with a network of autonomous drones, sensors, and digital command systems. The Air Force’s decision to choose Boeing over Lockheed reflects deep strategic reasoning: diversifying the defense industrial base, accelerating delivery timelines, and embracing a new model for crewed-uncrewed teaming.

When NGAD was announced, the Air Force described it not as a single aircraft but as a system: a crewed fighter working alongside autonomous drones, the so-called Collaborative Combat Aircraft, or CCA. The goal was simple on paper but immense in practice: create a crewed 'quarterback' that could control multiple uncrewed wingmen, each carrying sensors, weapons, or jammers, and all operating as one coordinated swarm.

By early 2025, both Boeing and Lockheed Martin had submitted designs. Each promised stealth, range, and intelligence far beyond anything flying today, and, on March 21, 2025, the Air Force made it official: Boeing’s entry, now called the F-47, had won. One of the strong points of Boeing’s proposal was its level of digital maturity.

Engineers had already built a full-scale 'digital twin,' allowing the Air Force to analyze everything from radar signature to maintainability before the prototype flies. That reduced risk in ways Lockheed’s more experimental design couldn’t match. Lockheed’s response was swift and pragmatic. Within days, the company said it would double down on its existing F-35 fleet, promising upgrades that could deliver “80% of F-47 capability at half the cost.” It was a clear pivot, and a quiet acknowledgment that, this time, Boeing had outpaced it.

For Boeing, the moment was redemptive. After years of negative headlines, from the Boeing 737 MAX crisis to KC-46 Pegasus tanker delays, this win gave its defense arm a new flagship and a morale boost it sorely needed. For the Air Force, it was a rebalancing act, ending a 25-year era of Lockheed dominance and giving Boeing a chance to lead again in the stealth arena.

The Air Force’s choice wasn’t purely about aircraft design; it was also about industrial strategy. For years, Pentagon officials have warned that too much of America’s fighter production capacity was concentrated on a single contractor. With Lockheed building both the F-22 andF-35, the Department of Defense risked over-dependence on one supplier.

Awarding the F-47 to Boeing was a deliberate move to diversify the defense industrial base. This is a principle often emphasized in congressional oversight reports and echoed by The Washington Post, which noted that “the decision also diversifies the production of US military jets."

Second came the issue of program maturity and risk reduction. Boeing’s design was built upon years of X-plane testing sponsored by DARPA. Those experimental aircraft, which explored adaptive engines, advanced stealth materials, and AI-driven flight control, paved the way for the NGAD platform. That gave Boeing a measurable lead in readiness.

Third was strategic urgency: since China and Russia were developing their own next-generation fighters, such as China's J-20B and J-35 and Russia’s Su-57M and Su-75 concept, the Air Force needed speed as much as stealth. Budget documents for Fiscal Year 2026 allocate nearly US $3.5 billion to continue F-47 development, marking it as a top priority.

By contrast, the US Navy’s parallel sixth-generation effort, the F/A-XX, has been scaled back to focus resources on the Air Force’s program. Boeing desperately needed a long-term defense anchor to offset its civil-aviation troubles. The F-47 contract provided precisely that: a chance to rebuild credibility, stabilize its St Louis fighter plant, and attract a new generation of engineering talent.

Lockheed, in turn, would refocus on upgrades and exports. In short, Boeing won not just because it had the better airplane, but because it offered a lower-risk, higher-readiness path to production. Awarding the contract to Boeing also better served US industrial and strategic interests.

Discover why the F-35 is the US Air Force’s most critical fighter — from stealth and sensors to strategy, readiness, and future upgrades

According to the USAF announcement, the F-47 is designed to deliver “lethal, next-generation technologies to ensure air superiority for the Joint Force in any conflict.” On the operational side, the F-47 is expected to combine deep-penetration stealth with long-range, modular systems and the ability to work hand-in-hand with drones.

It will likely feature radar-absorbent composites more advanced than the F-35’s, adaptive intakes that hide its engine face. It will also have a new generation of sensors capable of fusing battlefield data across land, sea, air, and space domains. Another one of the hallmark concepts is that the F-47 will not fly alone but act as a 'quarterback' to multiple drone wingmen that extend its reach and capability.

In terms of range, future fights in the Pacific could stretch thousands of miles from safe bases. That’s why the Air Force insisted on a new adaptive-cycle engine, co-developed by GE Aerospace andPratt & Whitney, that adjusts airflow for efficiency or thrust as needed. Given the pace of technological change, the platform must accept upgrades to sensors, propulsion, and weapons without a full redesign.

FAA budget documents and USAF commentary point to this as a critical element. While specific performance markers are classified, reports suggest a first flight targeted for 2028 and operations by the early 2030s. All of these factors make the F-47 less a single aircraft and more a platform for future combat concepts. It will be adaptable, updatable, and deeply connected to its uncrewed teammates.

Developing a sixth-generation fighter is not cheap or simple. The Air Force’s 2026 budget allocates around $3.5 billion to keep F-47 work moving, part of what analysts estimate will exceed $20 billion before production.

Most of that will flow through Boeing’sSt Louis plant, which already builds the F-15EX and T-7A Red Hawk. The use of digital-twin modeling allows engineers to predict manufacturing issues before physical testing begins, which is one reason why officials believe Boeing can deliver faster.

Specifications (Per The War Zone, The National Interest, af.mil, The Strategist, militaryfactory.com, National Security Journal)

USAF graphic posted by Gen. David Allvin indicates ~185 units.

1,000+ nautical miles (≈ 1,150+ mi / ~1,850+ km)

Cited in USAF graphic and press commentary.

The public commentary cites 'Mach 2+' for F-47.

Labeled 'Stealth ++' (vs F-22 'Stealth +' / F-35 'Stealth')

From the analysis of USAF graphics and reporting.

Several sources point to a 2028 first flight timeframe.

Industry reporting expects service entry in the early 2030s.

Approximately ~160 kN (≈ 35,000 lb) / Variable-cycle turbofan

Analysis of engine tech for F-47 suggests ~160 kN class for 'scaled-core' engines.

Crewed 'quarterback' fighter commanding uncrewed wingmen

Lockheed, for its part, is taking a different route, by modernizing the F-35 into what it calls a 'fifth-generation-plus' fighter. In a recent earnings call, its CEO described this as a 'value equation,' delivering near-NGAD capabilities at half the price for allied customers. That means Lockheed remains the export leader, even as Boeing takes the US lead in technology for now.

The Air Force's sixth-gen NGAD fighter continues to face an uncertain future with the Trump Administration's decision still pending.

Lockheed Martin may have lost the F-47, but it hasn’t lost relevance. The company’s pivot toward upgrading the F-35 shows strategic awareness, as the global market for advanced fighters is still growing, but not every country can afford a sixth-generation jet. What emerges is a two-tier structure.

Boeing leads the top end, with a handful of F-47s built for the US and possibly select allies like Japan or the UK. Lockheed, meanwhile, dominates the broader export field, offering upgraded F-35s to dozens of nations. For Boeing, this is a once-in-a-generation opportunity to reestablish itself as a fighter powerhouse

Air-dominance 'quarterback' with drone integration

Multirole export platform with incremental modernization

Fort Worth (US), Cameri (Italy), Nagoya (Japan)

Ongoing – upgraded variants through the 2040s

Limited — potential sales to close allies (Japan, UK)

Broad — available to NATO and Indo-Pacific partners

Long-range penetration, AI-enabled command of uncrewed assets

Affordability, sustainment, and incremental tech insertion

For Lockheed, it’s a chance to turn the F-35 into a long-term franchise, much like the F-16 was for decades. Meanwhile, for the US government, it’s proof that competition still drives innovation, even in a market dominated by two giants.

For aviation and defence watchers, this means we might see a two-track paradigm: one platform for highest-end threats (sixth-generation), and another for more cost-effective, transition or export applications. The effect on prices, supply chains, and global competitiveness could be substantial.

The road to service will be long but consequential. Boeing and theUnited States Air Force expect the F-47 to fly by 2028 and enter service in the early 2030s. Once operational, it will gradually take over the air-superiority mission from the F-22, likely flying alongside F-35s and drone formations in mixed packages.

When that happens, tactics will change. The F-47 won’t dogfight in the traditional sense, but it will direct others that do. Acting as a command node, it can send uncrewed aircraft ahead to probe defenses, jam sensors, or fire long-range missiles. Exports are possible but uncertain. Reports suggest Japan has expressed interest in an export-configured version, though such deals will depend on US policy.

If approved, they could mirror the F-35 model, with partners buying tailored versions that integrate with US systems but maintain security boundaries. For Boeing, the next challenge is industrial: scaling up production, modernizing its St Louis facilities, and managing a new generation of suppliers.

The Air Force will have to manage the task to ensure the F-47, its drones, and existing fleets will talk to each other. More broadly, the F-47 sends a message to adversaries and allies alike: America is moving fast again. After years of drawn-out development cycles, the Air Force is betting on agility, in both design and strategy.

#6185. Amex Business Platinum Card Bonus: As High As 300K Points Welcome Offer

The Business Platinum Card® from American Express is one of the most perks-rich business cards out there, and is useful if you’re looking to earn Amex Membership Rewards points.

We’re currently seeing a massive elevated welcome offer on the Amex Business Platinum, making it an ideal time to apply. If you’re eligible for this card and the highest possible bonus, it’s absolutely worth taking advantage of, in my opinion.

Link: Learn more about The Business Platinum Card® from American Express

The Amex Business Platinum Card currently has a massive welcome offer that’s as high as 300,000 Membership Rewards points after spending $20,000 within the first three months. Welcome offers vary and you may not be eligible for an offer.

Based on my latest miles & points valuations, I consider Membership Rewards points to be worth 1.7 cents each. This means that to me, the 300,000 points are worth a staggering $5,100. As I see it, that’s basically the best welcome offer you’ll find on any card.

Let me emphasize that Amex uses a variety of factors when deciding what offer people are eligible for, including history of opening and closing cards with Amex, spending history with Amex, how many welcome offers people have earned, etc. So, how does this Amex Business Platinum Card bonus actually work?

You should find the highest possible Amex Business Platinum bonus through the above link. However, if you don’t, it can always be worth checking refer-a-friend links, opting in to targeted emails from Amex, or even using the CardMatch tool to see what you’re eligible for there.

That being said, don’t expect to get a higher offer through any of those sources, since offers are typically targeted based on the person, rather than the application method. However, it can always be worth checking back every so often, because the promotions people are targeted for can change over time.

The Amex Business Platinum bonus spending requirement is potentially significant, as it averages out to nearly $6,700 per month. However, there are lots of ways to be creative with reaching minimum spending, and to make a plan. You could time your application around some large upcoming business expenses (whether that’s an ad campaign or buying inventory), prepay for some items, and maybe even put some expenses on credit cards that you might otherwise pay for with cash. Of course make sure you pay off everything in full by the payment due date, so that you don’t get stuck paying high interest charges.

Upon completing minimum spending, bonus points will officially post after 8-12 weeks, though in practice, typically post much faster than that.

There are lots of great uses for Amex points, as they can be transferred to all kinds of useful airline and hotel partners. Also keep in mind that having this card lets you unlock the full value of Amex Pay With Points, potentially allowing you to get up to 1.54 cents of value per point toward the cost of airfare on a designated airline (this comes in the form of a 35% Pay with Points rebate, up to one million points per year). You could then use that redemption rate for all your linked Amex Membership Rewards cards.

Just to give a couple of examples of how much value those 300,000 Membership Rewards points could get you:

In line with Amex’s “once in a lifetime” rule, the welcome offer on the Amex Business Platinum Card isn’t available to those who currently have the card, or those who have had the card (or previous versions of the card) in the past. On top of that, Amex’s general card restrictions apply.

There are a few additional things to note:

Anecdotally, I find the Amex Business Platinum to be a pretty easy card to get approved for, and you can read about my experience applying here.

There’s not a consistent credit score you need to get approved for the Amex Business Platinum, though I’d hope to have a score in the “good” to “excellent” range, ideally 700+ points. However, people with lower scores have been approved, and people with higher scores have been rejected, as it’s one of only many factors that impacts card approval.

The Amex Business Platinum Card has a $895 annual fee (Rates & Fees). While this isn’t the most rewarding card in terms of the return on spending, it does have a huge number of valuable perks, ranging from lounge access, to credits, to elite status.

The way I view it, the credits can help offset the Amex Business Platinum annual fee, and then the lounge access and other benefits are the icing on the cake. Here are just some of the benefits (Enrollment is required for select benefits):

Just to give a sense of the immense value, below is a basic rundown of the Amex Business Platinum credits, which should for many people help offset the annual fee (Enrollment is required for select benefits).

Of particular note is that the card offers up to $600 per year in hotel credits, in the form of a $300 credit semi-annually, and largely helps with offsetting the annual fee. The Hotel Collection requires a minimum two-night stay. Effective January 1, 2027, Fine Hotels + Resorts® bookings will require a minimum two-night stay to be eligible for the Hotel Credit.

When it comes to the Amex Business Platinum rewards structure, the card offers:

There’s another incentive to put at least $250,000 in eligible purchases on the card each calendar year, as that unlocks the following credits, which can be worth up to $3,600:

Read a full review of the Amex Business Platinum Card here.

There’s currently an excellent Amex Business Platinum Card bonus, which is as high as 300,000 Membership Rewards points upon completing minimum spending. While the spending requirement is significant, so is the number of points you can earn, so this is worth it if you’re eligible, and can swing it.

This card offers all kinds of great perks that can help offset the annual fee, ranging from lounge access, to credits, to elite status, and more. You can even see what offer you’re eligible for on the card without a hard credit pull, so it’s worth seeing if you qualify, in my opinion.

#6183. American Airlines Pilot Arrested At Heathrow For Being Unfit To Fly And Having Cocaine

Every so often we’ll hear stories of pilots being arrested for showing up at the airport intoxicated. Well, here’s an even wilder story, about an American Airlines pilot who not only showed up at the airport unfit to fly, but also had cocaine on him.

View from the Wing flags a story about how on November 1, 2026, a 64-year-old pilot was arrested at London Heathrow Airport (LHR):

So this is sort of wild — not only was he under the influence of something (drugs or alcohol), but then he also had cocaine in his possession. That’s just next level irresponsibility.

It’s not clear how exactly all of this was discovered, in terms of the sequence of events. Was there just a random check, or was he acting erratically, authorities were alerted, and that’s when this all came to light? If so, it sounds like the first clue was how he was acting (which made him unfit to fly), and then presumably he was searched, which is when the cocaine may have been discovered.

This is just so beyond irresponsible. If he was already unfit to fly during boarding and had cocaine in his possession, was he going to consume that during the flight, or just take it home with him?

Keep in mind that in the United States, commercial pilots have to retire by their 65th birthday. So this guy was just weeks or months from retirement… what a sad way to end a career, as you can bet he won’t be flying again. One wonders if he was just trying to party a little before retirement, if this had been going on for some time, or what.

While the authorities haven’t identified the airline that this pilot works for (other than to say he works for a US airline), it’s not too hard to figure out. Based on his name (which I won’t post here, because he’s in enough trouble as is), it’s clear he’s an American Airlines pilot.

American had two flight cancelations out of Heathrow that day — one for flight AA85 to Chicago (ORD), and one for flight AA91 to Miami (MIA). It’s not clear which of those he was scheduled to fly on.

Under UK261 regulations, any passenger who ended up arriving at their final destination four or more hours late would be entitled to £520 ($690) in cash compensation. That’s on top of covering any reasonable expenses incurred. Admittedly some people may have been rebooked on other flights once this flight was axed, but at least a large percentage of passengers would presumably be eligible for this.

An American Airlines pilot who was close to retirement decided to end his career in a rather unfortunate way, as he was arrested at Heathrow for being unfit to fly, while also having cocaine in his possession. The lack of decent judgment shown here is beyond irresponsible, and I hope he gets the help he needs so he doesn’t ever endanger others in this way again. The good news for him is that he was within months of retirement anyway, so at least his “career” impact is pretty minimal.

What do you make of this American pilot being arrested?

#6181. Buy Etihad Guest Miles With 60% Bonus (2.0 Cents Each): Worth It?

Etihad Guest has just launched its latest promotion on buying miles, which is being marketed as the biggest offer of the year. With this, members can buy Etihad miles with a 60% bonus, which is an opportunity to acquire them for as little as two cents each.

Is that offer worth it? Let’s cover all the details, but I’ll say right away that I think this offer has fairly limited appeal, and you should only take advantage of this with a specific use in mind.

Link: Buy Etihad Guest miles with a bonus

Between 12:01AM GST on November 12 and 11:59PM GST on November 22, 2026, Etihad Guest is offering a bonus on purchased miles. The offer is tiered, and you get a bigger bonus the more miles you buy, as follows:

Note that purchased Etihad Guest miles post within 72 hours of completing the purchase (typically faster than that), and that purchased miles don’t count toward Etihad Guest elite status.

Etihad Guest ordinarily charges 3.2 cents per purchased mile, and there are no further taxes and fees. That’s before any bonuses or discount. With the 60% bonus, if you maxed out this promotion you’d receive a total of 320,000 Etihad Guest miles at a cost of $6,400, which is a rate of two cents per Etihad Guest mile.

Etihad Guest limits members to purchasing 200,000 miles per account per calendar year, before any bonuses. The exception is Etihad Guest Platinum members, who can purchase up to 300,000 miles per year, before any bonuses.

The current Etihad Guest buy miles promotion is described as the biggest offer of the year. To compare this to other offers we’ve seen so far this year, we’ve seen bonuses of 25-50% (2.56 cents to 2.13 cents per mile), as well as discounts of up to 35% (2.08 cents per mile).

As you can see, Etihad Guest’s current offer gives you the best cost per mile so far this year. However, Etihad isn’t exactly aggressive with selling miles, so it’s hard to get too excited about any of these amounts.

Etihad Guest mileage purchases are processed by points.com, meaning they don’t count as an airfare purchase for the purposes of credit card spending. Therefore I’d recommend using a card on which you’re trying to reach minimum spending, or otherwise a credit card that maximizes your return on everyday spending.

See this post for more on which credit cards are best for buying points.

There are lots of ways to redeem Etihad Guest miles. While the airline doesn’t belong to one of the major alliances, there are many ways to redeem the miles on both Etihad and on partner airlines.

Below you can find the award chart for travel exclusively on Etihad. The pricing is based on the one-way distance of travel. Note that these redemption rates are specifically for situations where there’s GuestSeat availability, which is Etihad’s capacity controlled, saver award space.

If you see higher award pricing than what’s listed below, that generally means there’s not saver award space, and redemptions won’t be a very good deal. Furthermore, in some situations you’ll find higher saver level award costs, including for travel in the carrier’s A380 first class.

Etihad Guest has a separate award chart for travel on partner airlines, which is also distance based, and you can find that below. This is based on the one-way distance, and you can’t mix airline partners on a single award.

The main reason to consider collecting Etihad Guest miles is because the program has access to a lot more Etihad award space than partner programs do. Partner programs, like American AAdvantage and Air France-KLM Flying Blue, typically only have access to a subset of premium cabin Etihad availability. Furthermore, if you want to fly in Etihad’s The Residence, your ticket needs to be issued by Etihad, so an Etihad Guest award redemption would qualify.

There are two major catches when it comes to Etihad Guest, in addition to not really having slam dunk redemption values:

I’d really only recommend buying Etihad Guest miles with a very specific use in mind, if you know what you’re doing.

Everyone will value mileage currencies differently. Based on my latest miles & points valuations, I consider Etihad Guest miles to be worth 1.1 cents each. I tend to value points pretty conservatively, and there are many ways to get more value from Etihad Guest miles than that.

Etihad Guest miles don’t expire as long as you have at least some account activity once every 18 months. Note that you can only reset the expiration of your miles by crediting a flight to the program every 18 months, so other activity wouldn’t help in that regard.

Keep in mind that there are many ways to earn Etihad Guest miles, so outright buying miles isn’t the only option. Etihad Guest also partners with select transferable points currencies. In the United States, you can move points to Etihad Guest at a 1:1 ratio from Bilt Rewards, Capital One, and Citi ThankYou, so that gives you quite a bit of flexibility.

Admittedly not everyone has access to credit cards in the United States, and some people may also prefer to just buy miles if they can acquire them at a reasonable cost.

Etihad Guest is selling miles with up to a 60% bonus, which is an opportunity to buy miles for as little as two cents each. This could be worth it if you have a specific use in mind, but Etihad Guest just seems rather unserious with its buy miles promotions, since the program isn’t that lucrative, in terms of redemption rates, and the policies for changing and canceling awards is also incredibly frustrating.

So for a vast majority of people, I’d recommend giving this offer a pass, unless you’ve done the math, and it checks out.

Does anyone plan on buying Etihad Guest miles with this offer?

#6180. Where Does the U.S.-Israel Relationship Go from Here?

Opposition to Israel now has a toehold in both parties.

Israeli and American flags are flown at the March for Israel rally on the National Mall in Washington, D.C., November 14, 2023.

In the days since the midterms, it has become clear that the U.S.-Israel relationship is under assault in both parties. On the left, a group of DSA-linked Democrats has been elected to Congress. Like their precursor Zohran Mamdani in New York City and led by Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan, these new members place opposition to Israel at the center of their politics. It isn’t one concern among many but the defining issue of their candidacies. El-Sayed used his graceless and vengeful victory speech to attack Israel in barely disguised language: “Michiganders, we want our taxes spent here for schools here and health care here and infrastructure here. We don’t want our money sent to do apartheid or genocide or war.”

For the first time, both the Senate and the House will have — among the majority side — dedicated opponents of all aid to Israel, including even the sale of defensive weapons. They will see moves like an end to military assistance as weak half-measures, when much more must be demanded.

Israeli and American flags are flown at the March for Israel rally on the National Mall in Washington, D.C., November 14, 2023.

Business-class fliers on United Airlines will soon be able to relax in a fancy new Polaris Lounge at Denver International Airport (DEN).

Design work is underway on the new, exclusive lounge at DEN, Aaron McMillan, the managing director of hospitality programs at United, told TPG on Monday.

“We’re going to build a mezzanine on top of [the existing] mezzanine and expand the floor plate a little bit,” he said referring to a location at DEN near the end of Concourse A between gates A18 and A20. “We’ll have a two-story Polaris lounge there.”

United aims to open the new DEN Polaris Lounge by late 2028 or early 2029, added McMillan.

The news comes amid a club building spree by the airline. United opened a massive Washington, D.C.-inspired United Club in the new E Concourse at Washington Dulles International Airport (IAD) on Tuesday. The space is second in size only to the new club at Houston’s George Bush Intercontinental Airport (IAH) that opened in October.

United is also building a new club at San Francisco International Airport (SFO) that is scheduled to open by the end of the year, and is in talks for new clubs at Southwest Florida International Airport (RSW) in Fort Myers and Salt Lake City International Airport (SLC).

The Polaris Lounge is United’s premium airport space accessible only to fliers booked in same-day, long-haul business class or in business or first class on several partner airlines, including All Nippon Airways (ANA) and Lufthansa.

The spaces compete with American Airlines’ Flagship Lounges and Delta Air Lines’ Delta One Lounges.

United has six Polaris Lounges: Chicago O’Hare International Airport (ORD), IAH, Los Angeles International Airport (LAX), Newark Liberty International Airport (EWR), SFO and IAD.

DEN is United’s only mainland U.S. hub without a Polaris Lounge.

When United opened its first Polaris space at ORD in 2016, lounges were only planned at its main international gateways and not DEN. The Colorado hub boasted only one long-haul nonstop at the time: Tokyo’s Narita Airport (NRT), schedule data from aviation analytics firm Cirium shows.

Today, United flies five intercontinental routes from DEN: Frankfurt Airport (FRA), London’s Heathrow Airport (LHR), Munich Airport (MUC), Rome Fiumicino Leonardo da Vinci International Airport (FCO) and NRT. It will add its sixth route, to Paris Charles de Gaulle Airport (CDG), next summer.

“Aside from the local departures we’ve grown out of Denver, there’s also a fairly significant number of local customers that are connecting over like Chicago, and Houston, and San Francisco that are traveling Polaris that can take advantage of the product,” said McMillan.

And while McMillan was mum on the look and feel of the new Polaris Lounge at DEN, he was confident in one thing: it will not have an outdoor patio.

All travelers at DEN have access to the public outdoor patios at the ends of concourses A, B and C.

#6178. World Of Hyatt Brand Explorer: Free Night Awards For Staying At New Brands

There are several ways to earn World of Hyatt free night award awards. In this post, I’d like to talk about one of the often overlooked ways to earn Hyatt free nights, which is with World of Hyatt’s ongoing Brand Explorer promotion.

This offers World of Hyatt members the opportunity to earn free night awards for exploring Hyatt’s portfolio. Given the huge brand inflation that Hyatt has seen in recent years, this can potentially offer up to seven free night awards, and counting.

With World of Hyatt’s Brand Explorer promotion, you can earn a Category 1-4 free night certificate for every five unique Hyatt brands you stay at. When it comes to earning Hyatt Brand Explorer free night awards, here’s what you should know:

If you want to see how many Hyatt brands you’ve stayed at, you can do so either through the World of Hyatt website or mobile app. Just go to the “Brand Explorer” section, and there will be a display showing how many unique brands you’ve stayed at (including which ones), and also how many free night certificates you’ve earned.

When it comes to redeeming Hyatt Brand Explorer free night awards, here’s what you should know:

Of course you’ll maximize value with Brand Explorer by redeeming your free night award at an eligible Hyatt property when the cash rate would be as high as possible. World of Hyatt Category 4 properties can cost as much as 25,000 points per night, and in some situations, could retail for over $300 per night. So if you can find a hotel anywhere in that range, it’s a great way to maximize value.

Hyatt currently has 38 brands, which are as follows:

So as you can see, you’d need to stay at 35 brands to earn seven free night awards. If/when Hyatt adds two more brands, it’ll be possible to earn eight free night awards.

The World of Hyatt Brand Explorer offer is a fun way for the program to engage members and try to get them to try more brands. At least in one case it impacted where I chose to stay, because I do love checking this dashboard every so often, both to see the progress that I’m making, and be reminded of all the brands I’ve stayed at.

Even though I’ve had top tier status with World of Hyatt for over a decade and have now earned lifetime Globalist status, I haven’t even stayed at half of Hyatt’s current brand portfolio. As a matter of fact, I’ve only stayed at 13 of the 38 brands, so that’s just over one-third of properties.

Looking at the Hyatt brands I haven’t stayed at, most of them are all-inclusives, as that’s an area where Hyatt is growing significantly. However, in general this has limited appeal to me, based on the type of travel that I do. I’m sure I’ll knock out a few more brands in the coming years — maybe I’ll get to 15 brands, though I doubt I’ll make it to 20 brands in the foreseeable future.

With World of Hyatt’s ongoing Brand Explorer promotion, you can earn a free Category 1-4 free night awards for every five Hyatt brands you stay at. This is a way to earn up to seven free nights over time, based on Hyatt’s current portfolio of 38 brands. As Hyatt’s portfolio continues to grow, the opportunities to earn free nights continues to increase.

However, staying at Hyatt’s all-inclusive properties requires some effort, given that they’re not typically places you just drop into for a night.

Given how easy Hyatt makes it to track this, I’m curious — how many Hyatt brands have you stayed at? Which OMAAT reader has the record for the most brands?
