#6176. Air Algerie Business Class Review: An Odd Avion Express Airbus A320 Wet Lease

For the next portion of my Orient Express adventure via Africa trip, I flew Air Algerie’s Airbus A320 business class on the one-hour flight from Algiers (ALG) to Tunis (TUN). Okay, Air Algerie doesn’t actually operate A320s, so this flight was operated by Lithuanian and Maltese charter operator Avion Express (which Air Algerie is really bad at disclosing during the booking process).

I mean, what can one really say about this flight, especially after coming off of Air Algerie’s A330neo business class, which was possibly the worst long haul business class I’ve ever flown? Truth be told, for a short haul flight this wasn’t terrible, but it also wasn’t good. It was just… whatever. As an aviation geek, I always do love a wet lease adventure!

As I explained in the last installment, I booked an attractive one-way business class cash fare on Air Algerie, even though it didn’t start or end where I actually wanted to go. 😉 I booked the following in business class for $1,171 in cash:

10/03 AH2701 Montreal to Algiers departing 4:10PM arriving 5:00AM (+1 day)10/04 AH4000 Algiers to Tunis departing 7:10AM arriving 8:30AM

So in the last installment I reviewed Air Algerie’s A330neo business class, and then this installment is my review of the connecting flight.

I’ve already reviewed the Air Algerie VIP Lounge Algiers, which gives strong furniture store vibes and is nothing remarkable, but is still much better than Air Algerie’s onboard experience.

My flight to Tunis was scheduled to depart at 7:10AM, and my boarding pass indicated that boarding would start at 5:40AM. Yes, 90 minutes before departure… for an Airbus A320. Not surprisingly, that was completely inaccurate. I get that airlines don’t want people to miss flights, but I do find it frustrating when airlines don’t actually tell you when you should realistically be at the gate.

Anyway, my flight was departing from gate nine, roughly a five-minute walk from the lounge. Algiers Airport is fairly pleasant — it feels sterile and there’s not much to it, but compared to some other airports in the region, it isn’t half bad. But of course let me remind everyone that nothing holds a candle to Cairo Airport (CAI), easily one of the world’s finest facilities. 😉

I showed up at the departure gate plenty early, but even by 6:10AM (30 minutes after the alleged boarding start time), there wasn’t actually anyone at the gate.

The crew showed up at around 6:20AM, and boarding actually started at 6:35AM. The boarding process was rather strange on a variety of levels.

For one, before boarding started, the gate agent and security staff walked onto the jet bridge and then lit a cigarette and smoked. Nice… real professional.

Second, when boarding did start, it was just a free for all, with no priority give to business class passengers.

Third, there were three separate passport and boarding pass checks on the jet bridge by airport police. So first the gate agent checked documents, then upon entering the jet bridge a security officer checked both, then 100 feet later another security officer did the same, and then at the door of the plane, another security officer checked. After all that hard work protecting us, they definitely deserve a cigarette!

At the forward door to the plane I was greeted by the crew, and then headed toward my seat. I was flying on an 18-year-old Avion Express Airbus A320 with the registration code 9H-AMJ. While Avion Express is a Lithuanian company, this plane was registered in Malta.

This A320 has seen quite some things, as it started its career in 2008 at Wizz Air Ukraine, then in 2015 it moved to the main Wizz Air fleet when the Ukrainian subsidiary shut down, and then in 2021 it was taken over by Avion Express. Since then, it has flown on a wet lease basis with carriers like Eurowings, British Airways, Viva, and more.

For those not familiar with the concept of wet leasing, this is when an airline leases out its plane to another airline, including the crews. So while it’s sold just like any other Air Algerie flight, and the catering is like any Air Algerie flight, the crew and planes are from Avion Express.

This Avion Express A320 had a total of 180 seats, spread across 30 rows in a 3-3 configuration. Unfortunately unlike most of Air Algerie’s own planes, this one didn’t have a dedicated business class cabin with different seats. Instead, the first three rows were designated as business class, and they just had economy seats with blocked middles. That means business class had the capacity for 12 passengers.

I assigned myself seat 3F, the window seat on the right side in the third (last) row. This was a pretty old school cabin, which is a double edged sword. On the plus side, this meant seats were well padded, which you don’t typically find nowadays, given the emphasis on slimline seats.

Legroom was okay when you consider these are really economy seats, so it could’ve been worse.

The seat had a standard tray table, which folded down from the seat in front.

Given how old school the cabin was, it definitely wasn’t in very good condition, though. I mean, just look at the liner inside the window, and how that was coming apart.

Also, given the age of the cabin, it was clear that nothing had really been updated — there were no power ports, there was no Wi-Fi, and there was no streaming entertainment. That’s of course not a huge issue for such a short flight, but I’m just trying to help people manage expectations here.

The overhead console was typical for an A320, and had individual air nozzles and reading lights.

The cabin stayed really empty — there were only two other commercial passengers, and then one pilot who seemed to be commuting to Tunisia, for whatever reason.

Boarding was really efficient, and wrapped up by 6:55AM, as the flight wasn’t very full. That was still 15 minutes before the scheduled departure time. Before departure, the crew came around with juice or water as pre-departure drinks. I opted for a water, and was also given a packaged refreshing towel.

Ironically enough, on this flight the safety demonstration was exclusively performed in English (compared to my previous Air Algerie flight, where it was in French and Arabic, but not in English).

At 7AM the main cabin door closed, and at 7:05AM we began our pushback (sorry for the quality of the pictures, as the windows were super dirty)…

On the taxi out, we saw another Avion Express A320, which looked identical to ours (we also had an all-white A320).

There were quite a few Air Algerie planes parked on the ramp, as very few seemed to actually be at gates. I’m not sure if Air Algerie’s aircraft utilization is just terrible, or what.

By 7:25AM we made it out to runway 23, and were immediately cleared for takeoff.

Our climb out was smooth, and I loved the views on departure… I wish I could’ve actually visited Algiers, but the visa situation is complicated (and after my review, I’m not sure they’d be happy to have me anyway). 😉

The seatbelt sign was turned off around five minutes after takeoff. At that point the crew closed the curtain between the cabin and galley, and got started with the service.

On this morning flight, breakfast was served. There was no choice, but I was served a hot dish with scrambled eggs, veggies, and some sort of meat. There was also a yogurt, a croissant, and a pastry, and additional bread rolls were offered (though I passed).

It sure seems like Air Algerie instructs Avion Express flight attendants to not deviate from their service protocol, which is to say that everything must simply be thrown on the tray, with zero effort put into presentation. 😉

So I couldn’t help but reorganize the tray a little bit, to make it look a little more presentable.

Drinks were also offered. I asked for a coffee, and it was a rather disgusting powdered coffee that I didn’t at all enjoy.

Before the descent, I checked out the lavatory, located at the front of the cabin. It was very basic and worn, though at least it wasn’t dirty.

Since this was a wet lease, the flight attendants onboard worked for Avion Express. I couldn’t actually figure out what country they were from (and they weren’t really friendly enough that I felt like being conversational). But anyway, they went through the motions, and weren’t rude, and they spoke a little bit of English (more than the Air Algerie crew on my previous flight).

There was also one Air Algerie flight attendant onboard, I guess to “oversee” the service, as is common with wet leases like this. In this case, he just plopped down in a business class seat and relaxed for most of the flight.

Around 30 minutes after takeoff, at roughly the halfway of the flight, the captain made an announcement, informing us we were at an altitude of 10,700 meters (35,000 feet), and that we’d be descending in around five minutes. Sure enough, we started our descent as planned, and the seatbelt sign was turned on 10 minutes after that.

The views on approach were gorgeous. Tunis is of course a coastal city on the Mediterranean Sea, so the views are tough to beat. I fondly remember my visit to Tunisia around a decade ago.

On our approach, we ended up flying out over the Mediterranean, and then circling back to land toward the south.

We ended up touching down on runway 19 at 8:25AM.

From there we had a short five-minute taxi to our arrival gate, where we pulled in at 8:30AM next to an Etihad A321LR (probably the nicest plane that serves the airport).

From there I cleared transit security, and had an extended layover, before connecting to Marseille (MRS) in Tunisair economy (due to a downgrade from business class).

My Air Algerie flight operated by an Avion Express A320 was perfectly whatever. For an hour-long flight, I thought the meal was quite good. However, the Avion Express A320 wasn’t terribly inspiring in terms of its modernness, seating, amenities, or service. So yeah, I don’t really have strong feelings on this one, other than appreciating that the flight was at least on schedule.

What do you make of Air Algerie business class, operated by an Avion Express A320?

#6174. Global Airlines Liquidating: The Senseless A380 Dream Finally Dies

Over the past few years, I’ve extensively covered Global Airlines, the strange “airline startup” that had a single Airbus A380, with which it wanted to bring back the “golden age” of travel. The carrier’s A380 has been parked since the spring of 2025, and just several months ago, I covered how the company faced several winding up petitions. Well, there’s now an update, which seems long overdue…

Public records in the UK show that Global Airlines has finally been given winding up orders, which is the equivalent of liquidation. This is in response to a petition that was filed on May 29, 2026, and a court approved that order on November 4, 2026. This has only been added to public records today, as there seems to be a one week period between when these decisions are made, and when they’re published for the public.

This means that a government officer from the Insolvency Service will now become the liquidator, and take control of the company, investigate its affairs and the conduct of directors, and collect whatever assets still exist for creditors. This means that the directors no longer have control of the company.

What’s amazing about this entire story is that in the spring of 2025, the company actually operated two roundtrip flights to New York out of Europe, for reasons that most of us couldn’t really make sense of. For that matter, this was part of a wet lease agreement with Portuguese charter company Hi-Fly, given that Global Airlines lacked its own operating certificate.

James Asquith, founder of Global Airlines, gate crashes travel guru Simon Calder's interview with Mike Graham.@james_asquith: "Did you get a cupcake?"@Iromg | @SimonCalder pic.twitter.com/etMVj1TcPu

Shortly after the A380 operated those flights, it entered long term storage, as it needed to undergo heavy maintenance, which costs millions of dollars. The company’s founder, James Asquith, had insisted that the reason the plane was parked for so long was due to delays with being able to get heavy maintenance.

Just months ago, Asquith suggested that the airline would be flying to the Maldives before the end of 2026, despite no progress having been made on the heavy maintenance front.

A post shared by Robyn Asquith (@robynasquith)

Obviously on the surface, the whole Global Airlines thing sounds a bit odd. But let me simply say that the public knows only a tiny fraction of what was really going on here. That’s true both in terms of what Asquith was showing investors to get them onboard with the concept, and also what he claimed the goals for the company were.

My skepticism with this concept wasn’t because I don’t like to see other people succeed, or because I’m against innovation, or anything like that. Instead, it’s because things aren’t always what they seem, and when you’re raising millions of dollars of other people’s money and selling them a dream, there has to be some chance of that actually becoming a reality.

Keep in mind that in 2025, Asquith appeared on The Times’ 40 richest people under 40 list, which claimed he had a net worth of £183 million, making him richer than Adele. Right.

I’d encourage those who just went along with Asquith to be a little introspective here. For example, when you have publications like SimpleFlying that publish things about Global Airlines without even an ounce of skepticism, and then you have people like Captain Chris who latch on to people like Asquith as if they’re Richard Branson (which he literally compared him to, while pointing out that he was proving the doubters wrong), that’s a problem.

A post shared by Captain Chris | Aviation Life (@captainchris)

Many people lost many millions of dollars on this venture. Now, I’d also encourage them to perhaps be a bit more careful next time. And if you just want to make a donation to someone with no expectation of any return, I’m also happy to wire you my bank account details. 😉

It’s the end of the road (or runway) for Global Airlines, as the A380 “airline” has had its winding up petition approved, meaning the company will now be liquidated. It was only a matter of time before this was going to happen, so I don’t think anyone will be surprised. Hopefully one day the entire story can come to light…

What do you make of Global Airlines liquidating?

Why was Nvidia viable for 30 years? It's easy to ridicule the premise. The financials behind it were more complicated than the simple speculation of AvGeeks who just fly BIS.

#6172. Binoche Triumphs over Feminism

The great French actress Juliette Binoche can look at the world around her so naturally that no matter what character she’s playing (whether in Rendezvous, Flight of the Red Balloon, Summer Hours, Certified Cop, Camille Claudel 1915, Let the Sunshine In, Winter Boy, The Taste of Things, or in her Oscar-winning role in The English Patient), she presents a woman in a mode of inquiry.

In Queen at Sea, Binoche portrays middle-aged Amanda, a Frenchwoman living in England who is juggling a marital separation, a teenage daughter, a professorship, and her aged and senile mother, for whom she is responsible. Each aspect of troubled conscience contributes to Amanda/Binoche’s natural beauty. Binoche is a French version of the intelligence and sophistication associated with Irene Dunne in such films as The Awful Truth, Theodora Goes Wild, and Unfinished Business.

The considerable dramatic conflicts in Queen at Sea would be chaotic without Binoche to guide us through. As devised and directed by American filmmaker Lance Hammer, Queen at Sea catches the obstacles faced by Amanda and those closest to her. Starting with Amanda’s shock when she checks in on her senescent mother Leslie (Anna Calder-Marshall) and stepfather Martin (Tom Courtenay), only to discover the seniors in flagrante delicto, Hammer’s method is both confrontational and complexly personal. Amanda reacts politically, calling in the state apparatus to resolve unexpected domestic issues. She’s alarmed by consensual sexuality that doesn’t meet her preference. “If we don’t get some help, it will overwhelm us,” she tells her stepfather, whose most eloquent response is to look at her with surprise, then steely anger.

Amanda interferes like the most aggravating Karen in contemporary cinema. But that’s precisely Hammer’s point and Binoche’s artistic venture. Queen at Sea brings to light the imperiousness of feminism that has seized contemporary Western life. Acting out of her own uncertainty, Amanda would be a dislikable pedant, except that she is steadfast and loving in her intentions toward her mother, her stepfather, and her daughter Sara (Florence Hunt) who, in Hammer’s balanced narrative contrast, is just beginning to discover her own sexual nature.

Queen at Sea is a schematic exercise from the first shot of the elderly Leslie and Martin slowly climbing up a public staircase. Everything is a negotiation with progress. That was also the problem with Hammer’s previous film, Ballast (2008), the condescending racial drama set in the American South. Since then, Hammer has been on an artistic sabbatical, teaching in academia until he made this second feature. Like Binoche, Hammer is also in a mode of inquiry, which comes through when Amanda, in professor-speak, belittles Martin’s intimacy with Leslie: “This disinhibition is a consequence of the disease eroding the areas of the brain used to keep the primal instincts in check.”

Martin responds rationally: “Why are you so keen to deprive her of something that gives her comfort, pleasure at a time in her life when she needs them most?” This is a genuinely difficult dilemma, such as few contemporary films have dared. Hammer achieves a level of respectable compassion, yet one can’t help longing for Mike Leigh to step in and rescue it all.

Queen at Sea raises an essential question: Must movies be variations on social issues, or personal experience? Hammer’s art-minded condescension was transparent in Ballast, but it’s more effective here in compositions that depict the emotional friction between Amanda and Sara through Mondrian squares and distance — the space observed on the retirement-home surveillance monitors that capture Leslie’s sexual abuse. Montages of Sara and her wild-haired friends exploring their sexuality pay homage to Brady Corbet’s The Brutalist. (The teens express their “fear of the sublime” while literally searching the world’s structure to find responsibility or freedom.) Through Amanda’s frustration, Lesley’s quiet, and Sara’s naïveté, Hammer probes the sexual intimacy that most feminist filmmakers don’t articulate. (Martin and the male experience are sidelined.)

That the politicization of cinema has been ruinous is apparent in how Queen at Sea improves on such age-themed films as of Away from Her, 45 Years, and Under the Skin. The empathic Hammer rejects the nihilism of Michael Haneke’s Amour, which Americans mistook for a geriatric love story. Inspired by an actress from the French tradition of sexual candor, an empath like Hammer can only provide a heroine who thinks her way past this era’s political clichés.

Armond White is National Review’s culture critic and the author of New Position: The Prince Chronicles and Make Spielberg Great Again: The Steven Spielberg Chronicles.

As soon as you apply for a credit card, your application is processed by a computer. You’ll typically receive one of three responses: immediate approval, some form of “pending” status or denial.

Receiving instant approval doesn’t guarantee that you can begin using your card immediately. If you receive instant approval, you may be able to view your card number right away; otherwise, you’ll usually need to wait until your physical card arrives in the mail before you can begin using it.

It can take five to 10 business days to get a new credit card after approval. However, that timeframe varies by card and issuer. For instance, American Express offers overnight shipping for its top-tier cards. Some issuers offer expedited shipping on request, but there’s no guarantee. You may need to pay when requesting expedited shipping from some banks (including Barclays).

Getting approved for a new credit card is exciting, but waiting a week or more for it to arrive in the mail isn't. Fortunately, some issuers let you start using your new card immediately after approval, either by providing an instant card number or by allowing you to add your card to a digital wallet.

That instant access can give you a head start on meeting the welcome bonus spending requirement, since the clock starts ticking as soon as your account is approved — not when your physical card arrives. It can also come in handy if you need to make a purchase right away, whether you're booking travel or taking advantage of a 0% introductory APR offer. For cobranded store credit cards, you may also receive a discount on your purchases, starting as soon as you use the card.

Here's a look at which major credit card issuers offer instant card numbers, digital wallet access or both.

Some issuers provide an instant card number, while others, like Chase, instead let eligible cardholders add their new card to a digital wallet immediately after approval. Both options let you start using your card before the physical version arrives.

While there are too many cards to list that offer instant card numbers or access, here are six of our top picks.

American Express provides your new account number immediately after your online application is approved, provided your identity can be verified.

The instant card number will be the same as the physical card you’ll get in the mail, but the four-digit card identification number on the front of the card will be different. Because of that, you may want to wait to set up recurring payments.

Note that instant card numbers for some cobranded cards may only be used with the cobranded company (like Delta, Hilton or Marriott).

In addition to instant numbers for new cardmembers, Amex gives existing cardmembers access to their card information when ordering replacement cards.

Most Amex personal and business cards offer instant card numbers; notable exclusions include the Amazon Business Card and the Amazon Business Prime Card.

#6170. 6 Reasons Why Citi Strata Elite Beats Amex Platinum And Sapphire Reserve

I receive compensation for content and many links on this blog. Be aware that websites may earn compensation when a customer clicks on a link, when an application is approved, or when an account is opened. Citibank is an advertising partner of this site, as is American Express, Chase, Capital One, and others. Any opinions expressed in this post are my own, and have not been reviewed, approved, or endorsed by my advertising partners. I do not write about all offers that are available -- instead focusing on miles, points, and cash back (and currencies that can be converted into the same). Terms apply to the offers and benefits listed on this page.

Citi Strata Elite earns 50% more points on unbonused spending than Amex Platinum or Chase Sapphire Reserve, and those points can become American Airlines miles. It also costs $200 – $300 less per year.

I’ve written a lot about the card’s enormous first-year value. But the more I’ve used the hotel benefit, the more I think there’s a case for the Citi Strata EliteSM Card (See rates and fees) beyond the initial bonus. Here are six things it does better than Amex Platinum and Sapphire Reserve – both excellent cards and I have them both.

Banks advertise how many transfer partners they have. A long list can include many I even actively avoid (Aeromexico, Thai Airways). Most banks are also limited in whom they can work with because major airline and hotel cobrand card agreements usually include exclusivity provisions that limit what competing banks can offer. American Express has Delta. Chase has United. Citi has American. Of those three, I’d take American AAdvantage. Strata Elite points transfer to American at 1:1. And American still offers some terrific partner redemptions. However, some of my best American redemptions are just regular domestic coach trips. I’ve written about getting 4 cents and even 8 cents per mile from economy awards. American will sometimes make a flight cheap in miles while keeping the cash fare high. You don’t need to want a first class suite halfway around the world to get value from this program. Citi still has international partners I want, including Air France KLM Flying Blue, Singapore Airlines and Qatar Airways. Chase’s Hyatt transfers are a real advantage on the hotel side. (I still wish Bank of America had its own transferable points program, with Alaska’s Atmos Rewards as a partner.) 2. The Hotel Credit Works Beyond A Short List Of Luxury Properties Strata Elite offers up to $300 off prepaid hotel stays of two nights or longer booked through Citi Travel each calendar year. The discount comes off when you book, and applies to the room cost before taxes and fees. You can use it at ordinary hotels and independent properties, without restricting yourself to a luxury collection. Amex Platinum’s $600 annual hotel credit is split into two $300 periods and requires Fine Hotels + Resorts or The Hotel Collection bookings. Sapphire Reserve’s $500 The Edit credit is limited to that collection, with a maximum of $250 per qualifying booking. Chase also has an additional 2026 hotel credit, but that one is restricted to selected brands. Those programs can provide real value through breakfast, property credits and hotel loyalty benefits. Citi’s advantage is the much broader choice of hotels where I can use the discount. And I haven’t found that using Citi’s credit requires giving back the savings through a higher room rate. In January, I compared the Marriott at LaGuardia Airport: Citi Travel was $156 before taxes, while Marriott’s own member rate was $176. That’s $20 less per night before applying the credit. I still compare the room and cancellation terms, but Citi Travel has been competitive or even cheaper. I’ve also had little difficulty getting Marriott hotels to add my Bonvoy number at check-in and honor on-property benefits. Earlier this year I used the Strata Elite credit at a Marriott and received club lounge access. I similarly had no problem getting status recognition on a bank portal booking at a Westin this month. These third-party bookings generally aren’t supposed to be eligible for hotel points, elite-night credit or elite benefits. 3. It’s A Better Card For Everyday Spending Strata Elite earns 1.5 points per dollar on spending outside its bonus categories. Sapphire Reserve and Amex Platinum earn just one. You can do better with any bank pairing its primary card with a second card that offers different earn. Generally you’re permitted to pool those points. 4. Six Points Per Dollar On Weekend Evening Dining Is Fantastic Citi Nights earns six points per dollar at restaurants from 6 p.m. Friday until 6 a.m. Saturday, and again from 6 p.m. Saturday until 6 a.m. Sunday, all times Eastern. This works at restaurants generally, including qualifying restaurant delivery services. You don’t have to pick from a bank’s restaurant reservation list. Citi uses the time the purchase is authorized, so a Friday dinner doesn’t lose the bonus just because the charge posts on Monday. Outside Citi Nights, restaurant spending earns 3x. And Citi’s other big accelerators are 12x on hotels, car rentals and attractions booked through Citi Travel, and 6x on airfare booked there. You don’t earn points on the hotel spending covered by the $300 benefit. For airfare booked directly with an airline, Amex Platinum’s 5x and Sapphire Reserve’s 4x beat Citi’s 1.5x. Big Useful Credits Instead Of Many Small Ones I’ve laid out how to use the Strata Elite credits, but the basic approach is pretty simple: book a hotel stay and buy an American Airlines ticket. In addition to the $300 hotel benefit, there’s a $200 annual Splurge credit. Select American Airlines as one of your eligible merchants before purchasing, and a ticket billed directly by American qualifies. You don’t have to find incidental fees to use it on, as with Amex Platinum’s airline fee credit. The other choices are Best Buy, 1stDibs, Live Nation and Future Personal Training. You can activate up to two merchants at a time and use the credit over multiple eligible purchases. For me, American makes this easy. If the hotel benefit and Splurge credit replace $500 you’d have spent anyway, they leave just $95 of Citi’s $595 annual fee to cover. And both benefits run by calendar year, without dividing the money into monthly allowances. There’s also up to $200 a year for Blacklane, divided into $100 for January through June and $100 for July through December. 6. The Annual Fee Is Lower The annual fees are $595 for Citi Strata Elite vs $795 for Sapphire Reserve and $895 for Amex Platinum. You still get a premium travel card: Priority Pass lounge access with up to two guests, four Admirals Club passes each calendar year for eligible American or oneworld travel, travel protections, and up to $120 for a Global Entry or TSA PreCheck application every four years. And the first year still offers a lot. The current offer is 75,000 bonus points after spending $6,000 in the first three months. At 1.5 cents apiece, that’s $1,125 in points before counting what you earn from the spending itself. Someone opening the card now can use the hotel and Splurge benefits during the rest of 2026 and again in 2027, before their first anniversary. That’s up to $1,000 from those two benefits alone. If those credits replace spending you’d make anyway, the bonus plus the credits less the $595 fee comes to $1,530 in first-year value, before Blacklane, lounge access or points earned from purchases. Banks advertise how many transfer partners they have. A long list can include many I even actively avoid (Aeromexico, Thai Airways). Most banks are also limited in whom they can work with because major airline and hotel cobrand card agreements usually include exclusivity provisions that limit what competing banks can offer.

American Express has Delta. Chase has United. Citi has American. Of those three, I’d take American AAdvantage.

Strata Elite points transfer to American at 1:1. And American still offers some terrific partner redemptions. However, some of my best American redemptions are just regular domestic coach trips. I’ve written about getting 4 cents and even 8 cents per mile from economy awards. American will sometimes make a flight cheap in miles while keeping the cash fare high. You don’t need to want a first class suite halfway around the world to get value from this program.

Citi still has international partners I want, including Air France KLM Flying Blue, Singapore Airlines and Qatar Airways. Chase’s Hyatt transfers are a real advantage on the hotel side. (I still wish Bank of America had its own transferable points program, with Alaska’s Atmos Rewards as a partner.)

Strata Elite offers up to $300 off prepaid hotel stays of two nights or longer booked through Citi Travel each calendar year. The discount comes off when you book, and applies to the room cost before taxes and fees. You can use it at ordinary hotels and independent properties, without restricting yourself to a luxury collection. Amex Platinum’s $600 annual hotel credit is split into two $300 periods and requires Fine Hotels + Resorts or The Hotel Collection bookings. Sapphire Reserve’s $500 The Edit credit is limited to that collection, with a maximum of $250 per qualifying booking. Chase also has an additional 2026 hotel credit, but that one is restricted to selected brands. Those programs can provide real value through breakfast, property credits and hotel loyalty benefits. Citi’s advantage is the much broader choice of hotels where I can use the discount. And I haven’t found that using Citi’s credit requires giving back the savings through a higher room rate. In January, I compared the Marriott at LaGuardia Airport: Citi Travel was $156 before taxes, while Marriott’s own member rate was $176. That’s $20 less per night before applying the credit. I still compare the room and cancellation terms, but Citi Travel has been competitive or even cheaper. I’ve also had little difficulty getting Marriott hotels to add my Bonvoy number at check-in and honor on-property benefits. Earlier this year I used the Strata Elite credit at a Marriott and received club lounge access. I similarly had no problem getting status recognition on a bank portal booking at a Westin this month. These third-party bookings generally aren’t supposed to be eligible for hotel points, elite-night credit or elite benefits. 3. You can do better with any bank pairing its primary card with a second card that offers different earn. Generally you’re permitted to pool those points. 4. Six Points Per Dollar On Weekend Evening Dining Is Fantastic Citi Nights earns six points per dollar at restaurants from 6 p.m. Friday until 6 a.m. Saturday, and again from 6 p.m. Saturday until 6 a.m. Sunday, all times Eastern. This works at restaurants generally, including qualifying restaurant delivery services. You don’t have to pick from a bank’s restaurant reservation list. Citi uses the time the purchase is authorized, so a Friday dinner doesn’t lose the bonus just because the charge posts on Monday. Outside Citi Nights, restaurant spending earns 3x. And Citi’s other big accelerators are 12x on hotels, car rentals and attractions booked through Citi Travel, and 6x on airfare booked there. You don’t earn points on the hotel spending covered by the $300 benefit. For airfare booked directly with an airline, Amex Platinum’s 5x and Sapphire Reserve’s 4x beat Citi’s 1.5x. But for year 2, the real question is “what does this card offer me that is worth putting up with getting value out of these coupons”.

Unless you eat out quite a bit on weekends, or you really value 4 AA passes, the answer is probably not a lot. For Amex and Chase, the answer is some hotel/car rental status together with lounges. Yes one can argue that overcrowding and food quality negate the value of those cards, but the lounges are nonetheless the pot of gold at the end of the coupon clipping rainbow.

Agree AA is a great transfer partner and still probably better than UA (although UA has actually been decent this year domestically), but can get the $95 Citi Strata Premier to unlock AA at 1:1. Pair that with a DoubleCash and you’ve got an ThankYou point earning machine.

And BofA announced transfers with Atmos coming in 2027, so your parenthetical is now almost a reality.

Card will be coming up for renewal soon. Really struggling on whether to keep it. While the math above makes sense, I’m not sure I can justify the annual fee to basically earn it back. AA miles are valuable to me, but I also like to earn Hyatt points through chase sapphire reserve.

That’s a BOLD claim, Gare-bear. I’d say, they’re all special, in their own ways. (Though, Amex Travel has the best options, FHR, etc.) Chase has the better transfer partners. Citi has… Citi Nights!

@Brian – I suspect that you are not alone in that analysis. The really crazy part is that instead of letting you downgrade to a Strata Premier and keeping you in the ecosystem, instead they are only offering $0 AF ATT and AA cards. Obviously they want to have folks keep their Elite’s, but quite a tactic from Citi.

@Peter — Seriously, the downgrade options are a joke. Like, gimme a sensible spend bonus to retain, and I’ll keep Citi Nights-ing for another year!

On the passes for the Admiral’s Club. The last two trips I made, all of the clubs had “Day Passes temporarily suspended” posted. I would guess that includes these passes. Just be aware that they might not always work

Best Buy sells physical Amazon and gas station gift cards in store that count for the Splurge Credit too. Good to have more brand options.

@Traveling Tim: Per a post yesterday on FM, if the day passes come from your Citi card, the pass(es) will still work. Again according to the post, if rejected, you remind the rep where the pass comes from. Personally, I don’t know.

I have a zillion American miles from those endless Barclays promotions. Keep booking flight flights and they keep canceling them. Atrocious airline

Oof. Gary. Listen. I’m as Citi Nights as they come, but isn’t it a bit tone deaf not posting this after 6PM EST on a Friday or Saturday evening? (@L737! Just a week away!)

I’m trying to decide if I should PC a useless AA card into this card. I had it previously, so not eligible for the SUB. But if I can still double dip the hotel and splurge credits, it might be worth it.

What I really want is the Strata Premier, but they won’t allow that as a PC.

I parked my IRA at Citi to get CitiGold banking tier. That makes the AF only $445, and gives you free banking services (ATM reimbursed, free checks, free wires, free safety deposit box). Also gives you Citi culture pass for numerous free museums, and $200 in free subscription services (Costco, Amazon Prime, Hulu, others). Also gets you better customer service.

Paired with a Custom cash or 2 if you were smart enough to grab them before it was shut down, and you have a sweet setup. Everything else goes on the DoubleCash.

Amex has nice lounges if you travel solo, but Citi lets you bring a friend or two along. And 12x on hotels in the portal is best in class. So is 6x on weekend dining.

The credits are great. Even Blacklane, which is expensive but underrated, I love the service. The other credits are super easy to use. As a coupon book goes, this one needs no spreadsheet.

Transfer partners are awesome, as good or better than Amex/Chase in many ways. Lastly, the card itself is beautiful. Perhaps the best one out there. I hope they continue to enhance it.

@Peter, I actually have the opposite problem.

With 2 large DC lines, a Strata. and a Custom Cash, I can’t product change anything to the Strata elite…or any AA card, for that matter.

Traveling Tim The Citi passes are not the same as day pass and are exempt from the exclusion of day passes. I sue mine when the sign is out everytime and the people at the counter say it’s not the same as a day pass and the day pass restriction does not apply. I don’t think I’ve ever not seen the sign up TBH.

#6164. U.S. Pilot Arrested At London Heathrow Airport, Admits Cocaine Possession—Passengers Owed Over $150,000 Compensation

A 64-year-old U.S. pilot arrested at London Heathrow has pleaded guilty to possessing cocaine. Wayne Sigler, from Louisiana, was remanded in custody and faces two additional charges involving alleged drunkenness or unfitness for duty. According to the BBC’s report of information confirmed by the Metropolitan Police, Sigler was arrested on Sunday, November 1. He appeared in court on Saturday, November 7, and pleaded guilty to possessing cocaine. His next hearing is scheduled for December 7 at Isleworth Crown Court. Those charges fall under the Railways and Transport Safety Act 2003. The law also covers preparing to fly, duties after reporting for work, and standby. The charges don’t establish that he flew passengers while impaired. Reporting on the incident doesn’t identify the airline or flight, and I can’t directly confirm this is the right individual but there’s a Wayne Sigler who identifies as an American Airlines pilot in federal campaign donation records, and online discussion pegs him as an American pilot who came to the airline via America West and US Airways. On November 1, American Airlines 39 to Miami and American AIrlines 91 to Chicago O’Hare were both cancelled, and American 85 to O’Hare departed nearly 5 hours late. What Delayed Passengers Are Owed A flight departing Heathrow is covered by U.K. passenger compensation rules regardless of where the airline is based. For a journey over 3,500 kilometers, such as London to the U.S., a qualifying arrival delay of more than four hours means £520 per person (~ US$690.42). A three-to-four-hour delay falls into the £260 band. An airline can avoid the compensation payment when extraordinary circumstances caused the disruption. But the U.K. Supreme Court’s 2024 decision in Lipton v BA Cityflyer rejected that defense in the case of a pilot’s illness. And paragraph 170 specifically addresses a pilot who drinks enough to be unfit to report for work. If that causes a cancellation, the court says the reason is “inherent in the airline’s activity and operations.” A plane with 250 passengers at £520 each would mean £130,000 in compensation or $172,500. There was a British Airways pilot who bragged about using cocaine during a Johannesburg layover. A flight attendant reported his messages, he was kept from operating the return flight, and the airline fired him. #6163. AI Will Dehumanize the Job Hunt

I had been raised on stories of how the go-getters get going. You show up, you demonstrate desire to work, you list your skills and your aptitude, and someone out there, desperate for good, reliable help, will give you a chance. Bob Iger was a weatherman in Ithaca, then in 1974 started as a studio supervisor — a very low-level production job. He built a reputation for hard work and eventually became the CEO of Disney. Barry Diller started in the William Morris Agency mailroom. He got curious about how the entertainment business worked and used free time to read the agency’s files. He would eventually rise to higher positions, invent the “Movie of the Week,” and go on to run Paramount and Fox. Often these stories involve finding an older, experienced person as a mentor. Sol Price, the founder of FedMart, took Jim Sinegal under his wing. Sinegal had started at FedMart by unloading mattresses at 18. Sinegal rose through the company and co-founded Costco. We have tear-jerking movies about this, such as The Pursuit of Happyness.

All those stories highlight that market relations, careers, and success are not just a kind of abstract exchange and extraction of value, but really stories of human endeavor, development, and relationships. The market isn’t just the exchange of “utils,” money, and labor; at its best, it is a kind of theater for human virtue and adventure. Greed, grasping, or manipulation are sinful; hard work, creativity, and the courage to put yourself out there are our participation in the great good work of Providence.

Michael Brendan Dougherty is a senior writer at National Review Online.

#6161. Rail To The Austin Airport Is Back On The Table—After Costs Soared And A Voter Bait-and-Switch

Austin’s airport used to be super convenient but it’s outgrown itself. There are just too many passengers for the size of the facility, at peak times it can be nearly body to body as you navigate through the terminal. What was once curb-to-gate in minutes, security wait times on peak travel days can be quite long. And traffic gets backed up heading into and out of the airport. There’s a long trek across the road and through a parking garage, up and down levels, to get to Uber or taxis. They’re building a new terminal and a new headhouse. The airport’s solution is to get (a lot) bigger. It will never recapture the ease of a smaller airport, and it’s going to mean more walking and showing up even earlier. One thing Austin doesn’t have is rail to the airport. Voters approved higher property taxes in 2020 to pay for it, but the cost of the project ballooned and train ambitions remained – but the airport connection got axed to save money. Now the mayor wants to start the process of planning again for a train to the airport. The much smaller light rail system now being developed will cost nearly double what was once estimated, even though it won’t reach the airport when it’s supposed to open in 2033. But since the airport is building an entirely new face to the facility, it makes sense to plan for how a train would approach and where the station would go. Plus, they’re going to be looking to have the airport pay for a portion of it. That’s part of what the mayor means when he talks about rail reaching the airport without new tax money. Mayor Kirk Watson lays out a three-mile extension of the planned train, mostly elevated, with a station at the airport. He says the Federal Transit Administration has agreed to a streamlined environmental review, and the next nine to twelve months will be spent working through costs and funding. His challenge is to deliver it “within our existing budget approved by voters – no new taxpayer dollars.” Latest #WatsonWire: It’s time to start the process to get rail to the airport. For years, our Austin Bergstrom International Airport (ABIA or AUS) operated beyond the capacity it was originally designed to accommodate. That’s a sign of success, and a reminder that we can’t build Austin’s future relying on infrastructure designed for its past. We need to envision a successful future and prepare for it. The “Journey With AUS” expansion project is delivering significant improvements in building the kind of airport a growing, globally connected city like Austin needs for decades to come. As we build a better airport, we also need to think about how we’re going to get people there to catch their flights and how to get them out of there to participate in our city. A world-class airport needs a multimodal, world-class transportation system to connect to it. Sure, we need to improve roadway access. And we also should give people more choices about how they travel. We need to have the same long-term vision for Austin light rail that we’ve had for ABIA. An airport rail connection has been part of Austin’s long-term transportation vision for years. With Journey with AUS, we have a chance to plan these projects strategically rather than trying to connect them after the fact. Until now, Austin Transit Partnership (ATP) has appropriately prioritized navigating the Federal Transit Administration (FTA) process for phase 1 of our system. This year, ATP received the important Record of Decision (ROD) from FTA and completed, in record time, the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA) process for phase 1. In addition to getting the ROD and completing the NEPA process, I’ve wanted all major design and construction contracts in place and assurance that all of our financial decision-making is guided by a financial stewardship protocol before ATP takes any other big next steps. We have the ROD, the NEPA process is complete, the major contracts are in place, and the financial stewardship protocol is being followed. With these important milestones met, we can now take a major step: ATP will start the planning activities for a potential extension to take Austin light rail all the way to the airport. Read more: https://t.co/JTYqnnRyEE — Mayor Kirk Watson (@KirkPWatson) November 10, 2026 Airport Rail Was Part Of What Voters Were Sold Austin rejected rail proposals in 2000 and 2014. The successful 2020 vote for a $7.1 billion project came when voters were home during the pandemic and governments were spending unprecedented sums on Covid relief. The city’s election explainer lays out a Blue Line running through downtown to the airport, an Orange Line connecting north and south Austin, and a downtown tunnel. There were also commuter rail and bus improvements, plus $300 million for housing intended to ‘prevent displacement’ along the transit corridors. The ballot itself pitched airport rail. Voters approved an additional 8.75 cents per $100 of taxable property value, described as $437.50 a year on a home with $500,000 of taxable value, with federal funding expected to cover about 45% of the cost. Then the rail cost estimate exploded. By 2022, the original rail component had gone from $5.8 billion to $10.3 billion. That was blamed on inflation, land costs and construction costs but it was also the result of design changes to add more undeground tunneling. Without enough money, the connection out to the airport was dropped. The train got chopped from 20 miles to 9.8 miles. 26 stations down to 15 It lost airport servic and a downtown subway And the cost went from $5.8 billion to $8.2 billion With opening delayed from a planned 2029 reaching the airport to 2033 without it. The airport got dropped from ‘phase one’ and became labeled a ‘preferred priority extension’ if additional funding materialized. Now The Idea Is To Have The Airport Pay For Part Of It The Mayor repeatedly connects the rail extension to the airport’s ‘Journey With AUS’ expansion program. Austin is rebuilding its terminal frontage, roads and parking arrangements. And it’s building a new concourse. This is when you want to reserve space for a rail station. Journey With AUS uses airport revenues, airport revenue bonds, passenger facility charges and federal aviation grants. The airport sold $1.18 billion in May and plans $4.2 billion more through 2030. That money is spoken for, but the city owns the airport and it generates tremendous revenue. There are limits on what it can do with the money – the federal government makes grants and doesn’t want that money diverted. However, In 2021, the FAA began allowing on-airport rail infrastructure to receive airport funding even when the broader line serves people who aren’t using the airport. And 2025 FAA guidance says airports can contribute to ground access projects, including facilities beyond airport the property, provided airport funds support the airport-related share. So the airport link can open up airport funds now, as well as avoiding duplicate construction. The mayor frames the effort as “no new taxpayer dollars” but that’s different from “no new airport dollars” and the airport is owned by taxpayers. The Rail System’s Financing May Be Illegal, But The Election Could Change That The city created a separate public nonprofit corporation to pay for the train, so that the city itself wouldn’t be the one incurring debt. Then it held an election about the property tax rate, instead of one authorizing the city to borrow a specified amount of money. The city collects the property taxes and transfers the money to the special corporation which issues and pays interest on the bonds. Normally, in Texas, the city would have to specify an amount of debt to raise. If they later wanted to take on more debt, they’d have to go back to voters. Instead, they raised taxes by a specified amount and dedicated that tax stream to the project. Basically the city isn’t issuing the bonds, and isn’t taking on debt. The city also says it transfers the money each year, but future city councils could just stop making the transfers (winky, winky). There’s no city debt so they didn’t have to follow state rules for the city issuing debt. So property taxes support the borrowing, but the city isn’t mkaing a binding multiyear promise. There’s no debt. The state’s attorney general said this was completely illegal and sued. But he ran for Senate. After being impeached for corruption. This is the guy who spent the nation’s 250th birthday outside the country on vacation with the girlfriend he cheated on his wife (a state senator!) with. And he was videotaped partying in Dubai with fugitives. So he lost, along with every other Republican running for statewide office. It’s unclear whether the new attorney general will drop the case. For now, whether the state can take a tax increase and use it in perpetuity for a project that has ever-increasing capital costs, and then pivot later to use the funds to subsidize operations, remains tied up in the courts. There’s also a citizen lawsuit over the project’s bait and switch. Voters agreed to the taxes for a project that was completely different than the one that the taxes are actually paying for. Mayor Kirk Watson lays out a three-mile extension of the planned train, mostly elevated, with a station at the airport. He says the Federal Transit Administration has agreed to a streamlined environmental review, and the next nine to twelve months will be spent working through costs and funding. His challenge is to deliver it “within our existing budget approved by voters – no new taxpayer dollars.”

Latest #WatsonWire: It’s time to start the process to get rail to the airport.

For years, our Austin Bergstrom International Airport (ABIA or AUS) operated beyond the capacity it was originally designed to accommodate. That’s a sign of success, and a reminder that we can’t build Austin’s future relying on infrastructure designed for its past.

We need to envision a successful future and prepare for it.

The “Journey With AUS” expansion project is delivering significant improvements in building the kind of airport a growing, globally connected city like Austin needs for decades to come.

As we build a better airport, we also need to think about how we’re going to get people there to catch their flights and how to get them out of there to participate in our city.

A world-class airport needs a multimodal, world-class transportation system to connect to it. Sure, we need to improve roadway access. And we also should give people more choices about how they travel.

We need to have the same long-term vision for Austin light rail that we’ve had for ABIA.

An airport rail connection has been part of Austin’s long-term transportation vision for years. With Journey with AUS, we have a chance to plan these projects strategically rather than trying to connect them after the fact.

Until now, Austin Transit Partnership (ATP) has appropriately prioritized navigating the Federal Transit Administration (FTA) process for phase 1 of our system. This year, ATP received the important Record of Decision (ROD) from FTA and completed, in record time, the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA) process for phase 1.

In addition to getting the ROD and completing the NEPA process, I’ve wanted all major design and construction contracts in place and assurance that all of our financial decision-making is guided by a financial stewardship protocol before ATP takes any other big next steps.

We have the ROD, the NEPA process is complete, the major contracts are in place, and the financial stewardship protocol is being followed.

With these important milestones met, we can now take a major step: ATP will start the planning activities for a potential extension to take Austin light rail all the way to the airport.

— Mayor Kirk Watson (@KirkPWatson) November 10, 2026

Austin rejected rail proposals in 2000 and 2014. The successful 2020 vote for a $7.1 billion project came when voters were home during the pandemic and governments were spending unprecedented sums on Covid relief. The city’s election explainer lays out a Blue Line running through downtown to the airport, an Orange Line connecting north and south Austin, and a downtown tunnel. There were also commuter rail and bus improvements, plus $300 million for housing intended to ‘prevent displacement’ along the transit corridors. The ballot itself pitched airport rail. Voters approved an additional 8.75 cents per $100 of taxable property value, described as $437.50 a year on a home with $500,000 of taxable value, with federal funding expected to cover about 45% of the cost. Then the rail cost estimate exploded. By 2022, the original rail component had gone from $5.8 billion to $10.3 billion. That was blamed on inflation, land costs and construction costs but it was also the result of design changes to add more undeground tunneling. Without enough money, the connection out to the airport was dropped. The train got chopped from 20 miles to 9.8 miles. 26 stations down to 15 It lost airport servic and a downtown subway And the cost went from $5.8 billion to $8.2 billion With opening delayed from a planned 2029 reaching the airport to 2033 without it. The airport got dropped from ‘phase one’ and became labeled a ‘preferred priority extension’ if additional funding materialized. Now The Idea Is To Have The Airport Pay For Part Of It The Mayor repeatedly connects the rail extension to the airport’s ‘Journey With AUS’ expansion program. Austin is rebuilding its terminal frontage, roads and parking arrangements. And it’s building a new concourse. This is when you want to reserve space for a rail station. Journey With AUS uses airport revenues, airport revenue bonds, passenger facility charges and federal aviation grants. The airport sold $1.18 billion in May and plans $4.2 billion more through 2030. That money is spoken for, but the city owns the airport and it generates tremendous revenue. There are limits on what it can do with the money – the federal government makes grants and doesn’t want that money diverted. However, In 2021, the FAA began allowing on-airport rail infrastructure to receive airport funding even when the broader line serves people who aren’t using the airport. And 2025 FAA guidance says airports can contribute to ground access projects, including facilities beyond airport the property, provided airport funds support the airport-related share. So the airport link can open up airport funds now, as well as avoiding duplicate construction. The mayor frames the effort as “no new taxpayer dollars” but that’s different from “no new airport dollars” and the airport is owned by taxpayers. The Rail System’s Financing May Be Illegal, But The Election Could Change That The city created a separate public nonprofit corporation to pay for the train, so that the city itself wouldn’t be the one incurring debt. Then it held an election about the property tax rate, instead of one authorizing the city to borrow a specified amount of money. The city collects the property taxes and transfers the money to the special corporation which issues and pays interest on the bonds. Normally, in Texas, the city would have to specify an amount of debt to raise. If they later wanted to take on more debt, they’d have to go back to voters. Instead, they raised taxes by a specified amount and dedicated that tax stream to the project. Basically the city isn’t issuing the bonds, and isn’t taking on debt. The city also says it transfers the money each year, but future city councils could just stop making the transfers (winky, winky). There’s no city debt so they didn’t have to follow state rules for the city issuing debt. So property taxes support the borrowing, but the city isn’t mkaing a binding multiyear promise. There’s no debt. The state’s attorney general said this was completely illegal and sued. But he ran for Senate. After being impeached for corruption. This is the guy who spent the nation’s 250th birthday outside the country on vacation with the girlfriend he cheated on his wife (a state senator!) with. And he was videotaped partying in Dubai with fugitives. So he lost, along with every other Republican running for statewide office. It’s unclear whether the new attorney general will drop the case. For now, whether the state can take a tax increase and use it in perpetuity for a project that has ever-increasing capital costs, and then pivot later to use the funds to subsidize operations, remains tied up in the courts. There’s also a citizen lawsuit over the project’s bait and switch. Voters agreed to the taxes for a project that was completely different than the one that the taxes are actually paying for. Back in 2016 when I first started traveling to Austin frequently, the airport was one of the easier destinations to get in and out of. Then they moved Uber and Lyft to the remote parking lot 4 city blocks from the terminal doors and causing you to have drag your baggage upstairs, or downstairs to get to the pickup area depending on what level you exited the terminal. Not very convenient at all, and now, it has become very congested at times and all of the eating establishments and concessions are basically overrun at lunch, dinner, and breakfast. I hope they do the rebuild right.

The fundamental problem with light-rail systems is simple: How do people get from their homes to a rail stop?

If they have to drive (and park) there, they may as well just drive the rest of the way to their destination.

“ Voters agreed to the taxes for a project that was completely different than the one that the taxes are actually paying for.”

It’s quite common that driving & parking at a rail station then taking the train is far faster & cheaper than driving & parking at a major destination (such as an airport).

Voters never learn that transit systems always cost several times the original estimates while delivering less than promised. Austin’s results are nevertheless better than LAX’s people mover, let alone California’s high speed rail money pit. I thought that Oakland wasted $800 million on a BART connector to replace shuttle buses, but later projects are almost making that look like a bargain.

Too many make the mistake of believing the progressives when they say they want rail service to anywhere. They don’t really care if a single foot of track is ever laid down or not They only purpose of the rail projects is to siphon billions of dollars from taxpayers to well connected progressive companies and NGO’s. True in CA and LAX, and will be the same in Austin.

As they say history repeats itself. When SeaTac made it’s first renovation, it was more important to build parking garage adjacent to terminal then a light rail station. When light rail finally started is was projected so far over budget that federales were going pull funding. The City went back to taxpayers who swallowed and said ok. So, you can now take the light rail downtown to the airport painlessly(until you pay taxes on it).

Now, you can get on as far north as Lynwood(Everett planned). Also, you can go from UW to airport. And within the past year, you can go to and from Bellevue and Redmond(Microsoft hq). And that is a first by light rail over the Lake Washington floating bridge. A world’s first. So Gary, it only costs an unbelievable amount of taxpayer money.

1. Parking is extremely attractive target for miscreants, who know that the owners aren’t going to be back for a while. I’d prefer not to come back and find my catalytic converter, fuel tank or entire vehicle missing.

2. The same concerns also apply to the destination. Unless you’re going somewhere within quick walking distance, you’re going to need some sort of transportation after you get off the train. So, again, why not bring your own?

@D Fray Same experience, the trek to the rideshare lot is the worst part of AUS now. If you’re staying downtown, CapMetro’s Route 20 runs from the terminal into downtown for a couple of bucks, fine if you’re travelling light

The real issue with light rail (which nobody likes to talk about but is the #1 issue) is personal safety. The reality with most light rail systems (particularly at night but in some cities 24/7) is that there’s often a not-insignificant probability that you will be mugged, raped, or murdered. For the majority of people with the means to avoid light rail, they will do so, just like they avoid buses for the same reason. Just ask Iryna Zarutska.

RE: TexasTJ. LOL. I remember doing miles runs for early flights at JFK. When I got on the A train at around 4 AM, it was like a homeless hotel. I was like the only non-homeless on the train. I tried to find an empty place to sit. I was never robbed or assaulted, unless one considers unwashed odor as assault.

Also, I never actually missed a flight due to train stoppages. But I was always afraid I would.

However, I think the discussion about trains is kind of a red herring. The topic of the article, I think is about politician can handing out contracts and pay a lot of city workers on a train project. That is politicians are treating a train project as a loop-hole in the “no city debt” rules.

#6159. Hyatt Hotel Promises Jonathan Adler Toiletries—But There’s Drugstore Shampoo On Its Housekeeping Cart

Hotel Avante in Mountain View, California advertises Jonathan Adler bath amenities. A reader photographed its housekeeping cart with a retail bottle of HASK shampoo resting among unbranded squeeze bottles. This is another JdV by Hyatt property, just a few miles from the Wild Palms hotel where I reported on DRIFT bulk toiletries on housekeeping carts while the guest bathroom bottles displayed Jonathan Adler branding. Apparently readers need to keep checking what’s on the carts. The brown bottle is HASK Tea Tree Oil & Rosemary Invigorating Shampoo, in the 12-ounce size. HASK is an affordable retail hair care brand, with products sold at CVS and other stores. Around it are condiment-style squeeze bottles. At least one has “Body wash” handwritten on tape. That identifies the type of product, without telling guests whose product it is. It seems like Hyatt a good reason to check what this hotel is using to refill its toiletries. But they had this reason at its sister property, too. There needs to be much stronger monitoring. Hyatt’s Hotel Avante page lists “Jonathan Adler bath amenities” across all six room categories. The hotel’s separate website promises that as well. I have no particular opinion on HASK shampoo. My issue is that a hotel should deliver the product they specifically advertise to guests. And if the bulk toiletries in the room say they’re a specific brand, they should be that brand. The reader describes Avante as Wild Palms’ sister property and they’re both part of the same ownership group. In November 2025, I published a reader’s photos from Wild Palms. The bathroom had Jonathan Adler bottles, while the housekeeping cart carried large jugs of DRIFT Hydrated Body Care. Then in January, Ben at One Mile at a Time published follow-up photos showing the bulk jugs with their labels removed. Wild Palms still advertises Jonathan Adler toiletries. I just wrote about the ketchup, mustard and mayonnaise bottle approach to hotel toiletries. Once the hotel keeps reusing the branded packaging, it can change the contents without changing anything the guest sees. An owner who substitutes a cheaper product keeps the savings, while Hyatt and the advertised toiletry company risk their reputations. Remind me again why bulk dispensers were a better idea than single use biodegradable packaging? Hyatt’s Hotel Avante page lists “Jonathan Adler bath amenities” across all six room categories. The hotel’s separate website promises that as well.

I have no particular opinion on HASK shampoo. My issue is that a hotel should deliver the product they specifically advertise to guests. And if the bulk toiletries in the room say they’re a specific brand, they should be that brand.

The reader describes Avante as Wild Palms’ sister property and they’re both part of the same ownership group. In November 2025, I published a reader’s photos from Wild Palms. The bathroom had Jonathan Adler bottles, while the housekeeping cart carried large jugs of DRIFT Hydrated Body Care.

Then in January, Ben at One Mile at a Time published follow-up photos showing the bulk jugs with their labels removed. Wild Palms still advertises Jonathan Adler toiletries.

I just wrote about the ketchup, mustard and mayonnaise bottle approach to hotel toiletries. Once the hotel keeps reusing the branded packaging, it can change the contents without changing anything the guest sees. An owner who substitutes a cheaper product keeps the savings, while Hyatt and the advertised toiletry company risk their reputations. Remind me again why bulk dispensers were a better idea than single use biodegradable packaging?

More About Gary »

I understand the dismay of false advertising but does anyone really pick a hotel based on the shampoo or soap offered vs loyalty points, location, free/discounted parking and breakfast, and location? I’m seriously interested.

@Ray: Pretty much any legitimate brand of shampoo would be acceptable to me, but I still don’t find it acceptable to advertise one brand and refill the bottles with a different brand.

If the shampoo bottles in the shower were labeled Suave, and we saw bulk bottles of Suave on the housekeepers’ carts (in the original packaging from Unilever, not bottles with handwritten labels on tape), that would give me more confidence with regard to the hotel’s shampoo policy than what this Hyatt is doing.

It wasn’t. I have some sympathy for the environmental argument for the re-usable bottles, but corporate culture in the US showing [again] that they will take advantage of anything they can to save a buck. The bulk bottles on the wall were never a good idea, if for no other reason than hygene (who thinks they replace these once a year, if at all). But this is another reason. Taking advantage of customers, even at ‘luxury’ properties. Makes me wonder if we overvalue hotels and should just go straight to Fairfield Inn.

And these are just the instances we know about. If there are confirmed sightings of this in the past couple of months, imagine the actual scope of the problem, I assume this is going on at thousands of hotels.

If I were at Jonathan Adler, I’d start off by suing Hyatt for false marketing (or legal equivalent). For us guests, seems like it’s time to start pushing legislation that will force compliance. Require unopened, personal-size bottles of toiletries in every room. I have no problem with requiring it to be biodegradable, but even without this, seems reasonable from a hygiene standpoint. Even anllowing accurately labeled [bulk] bottles might be a slippery slope – if hotels have openly flouted that by using ‘ketchup’ bottles to refill, I imagine their reaction to comply might be to buy a single bulk bottle of advertised brand for each cart, then keep refilling that with the cheap sub.

On the other hand, maybe hotels would just revolt and stop providing these toiletries as amenities. As a traveller, might be a PITA to bring my own, but preferable to what seems to be going on now.

It all comes out of the same large industrial drum in the basement labeled “Universal Cleaner Base – 200 L – Made in China.”

@Emcampbe and others: It was NEVER about the environment. Never. It was ALWAYS about thinking of a way they could market sh*t and get people to accept it — even praise them for it.

We’ve seen that very thing in comments on in these forums: Person A complains about this sort of con-job, and Person B comes back with, “Hey, at least they’re trying to save the planet.”

I fully agree with @Emcampbe that the first step should be for Adler to sue them, arguing Hyatt is knowingly damaging their brand by passing off inferior products as theirs. If the neighborhood Piggly Wiggly starting putting name brand labels on cheap generics it would be an easy lawsuit. This is no different.

Why would a libertarian law professor have a toiletry brand?

One real issue here is that I have allergies to some brands and if they were substituted in and I didn’t know, my skin might break out.

I agree that the switch isn’t a good look. I just feel like is no benefit in advertising a brand. Just list shampoo supplied.

Of the chains, Hyatt properties are the most egregious offenders of using condiment-style bottles to squeeze unknown products into dispensers that are never cleaned or sanitized. I’ve even seen this at Grand Hyatt properties.

I think it’s high time the elites are forced to use these low-quality products.

I’m not a shampoo snob, I don’t have enough hair to be one but this can cause some real problems for people with alleges.

Some are allergic/ sensitive to tea tree oil. I bring my own products because I don’t want to worry about a reaction away from home. Most will never have an issue.

@Ray Not the shampoo itself, but if a hotel quietly swaps what it advertises I’d wonder what else on the listing is loose. For the stuff you mention I compare the full stay, room plus parking and breakfast, not the headline rate. FWIW free tools like Arbitrica or similar check the same hotel from a bunch of countries to find kind of the lowest price in the world, since rates and inventory differ by country. Then let location decide

@Matt — You know what would solve this… better consumer protections… *wink*

@Maryland — Tried to mention to you earlier this week, I finally made it to western PA. Thank you again for recommending.

1990 great. Snow moving in any time. So many acres. So sad. I cry thinking about it

No one who travels likes the large bottles in the shower. Who knows what people put into them. I travel with my own soap etc. I don’t want any surprises.

@RT – I’ve known Jonathan for 30 years, and he never mentioned it to me! 😉

There are real working solutions already employed by other industries for this problem that keep operators honest while still allowing multi use containers. Welcome to the stage Heinz ketchup.

That company that figured it all out and have pretty successfully stopped every trick in the book by restaurants trying to get away with refilling Heinz bottles with cheaper crappier products.

They do things like: – Sell large multi use bottles to restaurants but do not allowing refilling in their contracts, they must be replaced. – they have created dispenser systems that can only be refilled by replacing internal sealed bags that cant be refilled (those big Heinz branded condiment boxes you use the pump handle to get ketchup out of). – They give restaurants Heinz bottles that are always transparent and the label has a red outline around the ages that is perfectly color matched with Heinz ketchup so is largely invisible when filled with Heinz ketchup but sticks out clearly when the bottle is full of a different brand’s ketchup. – And most of all they aggressively audit restaurants and sue if they find violations. – Probably way more tricks of the trade then that too.

The toiletry brands should employ some of the same techniques with hotels, they are not that hard. As long as the hotel is not lying about it and keeping them sanitized I actually like the user experience of larger multi use products as I like liquid soap better then bars and you don’t run out if your sharing a room with another person.

@Maryland — It was so well-done. Lost it at the ‘tower of voices’… windy day; it was like they were singing. And how they included the child for Ms. Grancolas. The answering machines. Wow. (Winter isn’t all bad; would like to return, someday, maybe see Fallingwater in the snow.) Take care out there.

Love it. Hard core political discussions (vs. travel discussions) to shampoo snobbery.. A real eclectic site.

I was at the tower of voices before the actual opening. The place is spiritual. And falling water. Is part of my history. Try the Nemacolin resort nearby for an awesome array of summer activity. Who doesn’t want to drive hummers over rocks and shoot guns? Maggie also has another less expensive hotel nearby . They filmed that bachelor series there if you are looking for a date….always. Maryland

@Maryland — Aww! It really is. There was a school group when I was there; reminded me that these kids weren’t even alive when it happened. All sorts of ‘feels.’ Taking notes for next time. Saw a car with Maryland plates and a cute bumper sticker with “tell your dog I said hi” (Thought of you! Unlike Matthew, I love dogs…Bah!)

@Quinn…agreeed. If I was a brand promoted on the bottle and my product wasn’t in there, I’d sue them for sure. As someone mentioned, some people have allergies to specific ingredients. Not that the ingredients are necessarily on the labels in hotels, but those people probably have a good idea what brands to steer clear of. Would be great for someone to have a reaction, sue the product manufacturer and then find out it wasn’t their product.

All about the chip, chip, chip to keep increasing profits.
